questions.q: Octant of (−5, −3, 4) is
questions.why: The signs (−, −, +) correspond to octant III.

questions.q: The z-axis is given by
questions.why: The z-axis consists of the points where both x and y are zero, so it is given by x = 0, y = 0.

questions.q: Distance of (3, −4, 0) from the origin is
questions.why: Distance from the origin = √(3² + (−4)² + 0²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5.

questions.q: Distance of (4, −3, 5) from the ZX-plane is
questions.why: The distance from a point to the ZX-plane is the absolute value of its y-coordinate: |−3| = 3.

questions.q: Distance between (−1, 3, −4) and (1, −3, 4) is
Foot of the perpendicular from (−4, 3, 2) to the x-axis is
questions.why: The foot of the perpendicular on the x-axis keeps the x-coordinate and sets y and z to 0. For (−4, 3, 2) this gives (−4, 0, 0).

questions.q: Assertion: (0, 4, −3) lies in the YZ-plane. Reason: its x-coordinate is 0.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. The YZ-plane is x = 0, and the point (0, 4, −3) has x = 0, so the reason explains why it lies in that plane.

questions.q: If the distance between (a, 2, 1) and (1, −1, 1) is 5, then a =
questions.why: The distance condition gives (a − 1)² + 9 + 0 = 25, so (a − 1)² = 16 and a − 1 = ±4. That gives a = 5 or a = −3.

questions.q: The triangle with vertices (0, 0, 0), (2, 0, 0), (0, 2, 0) is
questions.why: The two legs from the origin each have length 2 and meet at a right angle at the origin. The hypotenuse is 2√2, so the triangle is right-angled isosceles.
The distance between consecutive points is √3 each, and between the end points it is √12 = 2√3. Since √3 + √3 = 2√3, the points lie on one line.

questions.q: Case: A lamp hangs at (2, 3, 4) m in a room with origin at a floor corner. Its height above the floor is
questions.why: With the origin at the floor corner, the z-coordinate is the height. So the lamp at (2, 3, 4) is 4 m above the floor.

questions.q: The locus of points equidistant from (1, 0, 0) and (−1, 0, 0) is
questions.why: Equal distances give (x − 1)² + y² + z² = (x + 1)² + y² + z². This simplifies to −2x = 2x, so x = 0, the YZ-plane.

questions.q: Find the point on the y-axis equidistant from (3, 1, 2) and (5, 5, 2).
questions.why: For (0, y, 0): 9 + (y − 1)² + 4 = 25 + (y − 5)² + 4. This simplifies to −2y + 14 = −10y + 54, so 8y = 40 and y = 5, giving (0, 5, 0).

questions.q: Locus of P with PA² + PB² = 2k² for A(3, 4, 5) and B(−1, 3, −7) is
questions.why: Expand PA² + PB² with P(x, y, z). The x², y², z² terms double, and the constant is 9 + 16 + 25 + 1 + 9 + 49 = 109. Setting it equal to 2k² gives the stated equation.
The distances are √14, 2√14 and 3√14, and √14 + 2√14 = 3√14. When two shorter distances add to the longest, the points lie on one straight line.

questions.q: A point P on the x-axis is at distance 13 from (0, 12, 5). Then P is
questions.why: A point P(x, 0, 0) on the x-axis is at distance √(x² + 12² + 5²) from (0, 12, 5). Setting this to 13 gives x² + 144 + 25 = 169, so x² = 0 and x = 0, i.e. P is the origin.

courses.title: Ch 12 · Limits and Derivatives
courses.summary: An intuitive idea of limits, left- and right-hand limits, algebra of limits, standard limits for polynomials, rational and trigonometric functions, the derivative from first principles and rules of differentiation.
outcomes: Learners can find limits by substitution, factorisation and rationalisation
Learners can use lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹ and lim sin x/x = 1
Learners can find derivatives from first principles
Learners can apply sum, product and quotient rules to polynomials and trigonometric functions

scenes.text: A car's speedometer shows speed *right now* — but speed is distance over time, and 'right now' has zero time.
We look at smaller and smaller time intervals and see what value the average speed approaches. That is a limit.

steps.title: Intuitive meaning
steps.body:
**lim (x→a) f(x) = l** means f(x) gets as close as we like to l when x is close enough to a (x ≠ a).

- **Left-hand limit** (x → a⁻) and **right-hand limit** (x → a⁺).
- The limit exists iff both exist and are equal.
- The limit need not equal f(a); f(a) may not even be defined.

steps.title: Solved example 2: one-sided
steps.body:
f(x) = x + 2 for x ≤ 1, and f(x) = 3x for x > 1. Does lim (x→1) f(x) exist?

- LHL = 1 + 2 = 3; RHL = 3(1) = 3. Equal → limit is **3**.

For g(x) = |x|/x at 0: LHL = −1, RHL = 1 → **no limit**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking 0/0 means the limit is 0 or does not exist — it is *indeterminate*; simplify first.
- Assuming lim f(x) = f(a) always.
- Checking only one side for piecewise functions.

statements.s: If f(a) is undefined, lim (x→a) f(x) cannot exist.
statements.why: (x² − 1)/(x − 1) is undefined at 1 but has limit 2.

statements.s: A limit exists only if LHL = RHL.
lim (x→0) |x|/x exists.
0/0 is called an indeterminate form.
For a polynomial p, lim (x→a) p(x) = p(a).

quiz.q: lim (x→3) (x + 3) is
quiz.why: The function x + 3 is continuous, so the limit is found by direct substitution: 3 + 3 = 6. There is no 0/0 problem to resolve.

quiz.q: lim (x→2) (x² − 4)/(x − 2) is
quiz.why: Direct substitution gives 0/0, so factorise: (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = (x − 2)(x + 2)/(x − 2) = x + 2. At x = 2 this is 4.

quiz.q: For f(x) = [x], lim (x→2⁻) f(x) is
quiz.why: The greatest integer function [x] is 1 for 1 ≤ x < 2. As x approaches 2 from the left (2⁻), values are just below 2, so [x] = 1.

quiz.q: If LHL = 5 and RHL = 5 at x = a and f(a) = 7, then lim (x→a) f(x) is
quiz.why: A limit depends only on the values near x = a, not on f(a) itself. Since the left and right limits are both 5, the limit is 5 even though f(a) = 7.

quiz.q: lim (x→1) (x³ − 1)/(x − 1) is
quiz.why: Factorise x³ − 1 = (x − 1)(x² + x + 1) and cancel (x − 1). The limit is x² + x + 1 at x = 1, which is 3.

lessons.title: Algebra of limits and standard limits

scenes.text: A complicated limit can be split into simpler limits — like splitting a big bill among friends.
The algebra of limits says how to split sums, products and quotients.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
If lim f = l and lim g = m (x → a):
- lim (f ± g) = l ± m; lim (fg) = lm; lim (kf) = kl
- lim (f/g) = l/m (m ≠ 0)

**Standard result:** **lim (x→a) (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = n aⁿ⁻¹**.

For rational functions, if substitution gives 0/0, factorise or rationalise.

steps.title: Solved example 2: standard result
steps.body:
lim (x→1) (x¹⁵ − 1)/(x¹⁰ − 1).

- Divide top and bottom by (x − 1): (15·1¹⁴)/(10·1⁹) = **3/2**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Splitting a quotient when the denominator's limit is 0.
- Cancelling (x − a) and then forgetting to substitute.
- Writing n aⁿ instead of n aⁿ⁻¹.

activity.prompt: Evaluate lim (x→2) (x⁵ − 32)/(x − 2).

quiz.q: lim (x→−1) (x¹⁰ + x⁵ + 1)/(x − 1) is
quiz.why: The denominator x − 1 is −2 at x = −1, not zero, so substitute directly: (1 − 1 + 1)/(−2) = −1/2, since (−1)¹⁰ = 1 and (−1)⁵ = −1.

quiz.q: lim (x→a) (x⁴ − a⁴)/(x − a) equals
quiz.why: Using the standard limit lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = n aⁿ⁻¹ with n = 4 gives 4a³.

quiz.q: lim (x→0) [(x + 1)⁵ − 1]/x is
quiz.why: Let y = x + 1, so y → 1. The limit becomes (y⁵ − 1)/(y − 1) → 5 · 1⁴ = 5. (It is also the derivative of (1 + x)⁵ at 0.)

quiz.q: lim (x→3) (x² − 9)/(x − 3) is
quiz.why: x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3), so after cancelling the limit is x + 3 = 6 at x = 3.
The denominator is 4 − 2 = 2, not zero, so direct substitution works: (4 × 4 + 3)/2 = 19/2.

scenes.text: Astronomers and engineers often replace sin x by x when the angle is tiny (in radians).
The reason is the famous limit sin x / x → 1.

steps.title: Two key limits (x in radians)
steps.body:
- **lim (x→0) sin x / x = 1** (proved with the sandwich theorem using areas in a unit circle: cos x < sin x/x < 1).
- **lim (x→0) (1 − cos x)/x = 0**.
- Consequences: lim sin(ax)/(bx) = a/b; lim tan x / x = 1.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
lim (x→0) (1 − cos 2x)/x².

- 1 − cos 2x = 2 sin²x.
- 2 (sin x/x)² → **2**.

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body: lim (x→0) tan x / x = lim (sin x/x)·(1/cos x) = 1 · 1 = **1**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using degrees: sin x/x → 1 only for radians.
- Writing lim sin 5x/x = 1 (it is 5).
- Forgetting that (1 − cos x)/x² → 1/2, not 0.

activity.prompt: Match each limit (x → 0) with its value.

quiz.q: lim (x→0) sin ax / sin bx is
quiz.why: Write sin ax/sin bx = (sin ax/ax)·(bx/sin bx)·(a/b). Both standard limits tend to 1, leaving a/b.

quiz.q: lim (x→0) x / tan x is
quiz.why: x/tan x is the reciprocal of tan x/x. Since tan x/x → 1 as x → 0, the limit is 1.

quiz.q: lim (x→0) (cos x − 1)/x is
quiz.why: (cos x − 1)/x = −(1 − cos x)/x, and (1 − cos x)/x → 0 as x → 0 (it behaves like x/2). So the limit is 0, not −1.

quiz.q: lim (x→π) sin(π − x)/(π(π − x)) is
quiz.why: Let h = π − x, so h → 0. The expression becomes sin h/(πh), and sin h/h → 1, giving 1/π.

quiz.q: lim (x→0) (cosec x − cot x) is
quiz.why: cosec x − cot x = (1 − cos x)/sin x = tan(x/2). As x → 0, tan(x/2) → 0.

scenes.text: A stone falls s(t) = 4.9t² metres in t seconds. How fast is it moving at t = 2 s?
Average speed over [2, 2 + h] approaches 19.6 m/s as h → 0 — the derivative.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
The **derivative** of f at a:
**f′(a) = lim (h→0) [f(a + h) − f(a)]/h**, if the limit exists.

The derivative function: f′(x) = lim (h→0) [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h; also written dy/dx or d/dx f(x). Geometrically it is the **slope of the tangent**; physically, an instantaneous rate of change.

steps.title: Solved example 1: f(x) = x² at x = 2
Solved example 3: sin x
steps.body: d/dx sin x = lim [sin(x + h) − sin x]/h = lim 2cos(x + h/2) sin(h/2)/h = cos x · 1 = **cos x**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expanding f(x + h) wrongly, e.g. (x + h)² = x² + h².
- Putting h = 0 before cancelling h (gives 0/0).
- Confusing f′(a) (a number) with f′(x) (a function).

activity.prompt: Using first principles, find the instantaneous speed (m/s) at t = 2 for s(t) = 4.9t².

quiz.q: Derivative of f(x) = 3x at any x is
quiz.why: From first principles [3(x + h) − 3x]/h = 3h/h = 3, so the derivative is the constant 3, the slope of the line y = 3x.

quiz.q: Derivative of a constant is
quiz.why: For a constant function f(x + h) − f(x) = 0, so the difference quotient is 0 and the derivative is 0 (a horizontal line has zero slope).

quiz.q: Geometrically, f′(a) is
options: slope of the tangent at x = a
quiz.why: The derivative f′(a) is the limit of slopes of secant lines as the second point approaches a, which is the slope of the tangent at x = a.

quiz.q: From first principles, d/dx (x³) is
quiz.why: (x + h)³ − x³ = 3x²h + 3xh² + h³. Dividing by h gives 3x² + 3xh + h², and as h → 0 this is 3x².

quiz.q: d/dx cos x from first principles is
quiz.why: Using cos(x + h) − cos x = −2 sin(x + h/2) sin(h/2), dividing by h and letting h → 0 gives −sin x.

scenes.text: A factory's cost is C(x) = 0.005x³ − 0.02x² + 30x + 5000. The manager wants the cost of one more unit at x = 3.
The derivative C′(x) — the marginal cost — answers it without first principles every time.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- d/dx xⁿ = n xⁿ⁻¹ (any integer n; also rational n)
- (u ± v)′ = u′ ± v′; (ku)′ = ku′
- **Product:** (uv)′ = u′v + uv′
- **Quotient:** (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v² (v ≠ 0)
- d/dx sin x = cos x; cos x → −sin x; tan x → sec²x; sec x → sec x tan x; cosec x → −cosec x cot x; cot x → −cosec²x.

steps.title: Solved example 1: product
steps.body: d/dx (x² sin x) = 2x sin x + x² cos x.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- (uv)′ ≠ u′v′.
- Swapping the order in the quotient rule numerator (u′v − uv′, not uv′ − u′v).
- d/dx cos x is −sin x (sign!).

steps.title: Polynomial shortcut
steps.body: d/dx (aₙxⁿ + … + a₁x + a₀) = naₙxⁿ⁻¹ + … + a₁.

activity.prompt: If f(x) = x³ − 4x + 7, find f′(2).

quiz.q: d/dx (5x⁴ − 3x + 2) is
quiz.why: Differentiate term by term: 5·4x³ = 20x³, −3x gives −3, and the constant 2 gives 0. So the derivative is 20x³ − 3.

quiz.q: d/dx (x sin x) is
quiz.why: By the product rule, (x)′ sin x + x (sin x)′ = sin x + x cos x.

quiz.q: d/dx tan x is
quiz.why: The standard result is d/dx (tan x) = sec²x. The expression −cosec²x is the derivative of cot x.

quiz.q: d/dx (1/x²) is
quiz.why: Write 1/x² as x⁻². The power rule gives −2x⁻³ = −2/x³.

quiz.q: d/dx (sin x / x) is
quiz.why: By the quotient rule, (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v² with u = sin x and v = x: (x cos x − sin x)/x².

questions.q: lim (x→2) (3x + 1) is
questions.why: 3x + 1 is continuous, so substitute x = 2: 3(2) + 1 = 7.

questions.q: lim (x→0) sin 5x / x is
questions.why: Write sin 5x/x = 5 · (sin 5x/5x). As x → 0, sin 5x/5x → 1, so the limit is 5.

questions.q: d/dx (x⁷) is
questions.why: By the power rule, d/dx (xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹. So d/dx (x⁷) = 7x⁶.

questions.q: lim (x→1) (x² − 1)/(x − 1) is
questions.why: x² − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1), so the quotient simplifies to x + 1, which is 2 at x = 1.

questions.q: d/dx (sin x + cos x) is
questions.why: Differentiate each term: (sin x)′ = cos x and (cos x)′ = −sin x. So the derivative is cos x − sin x.

questions.q: lim (x→0) (1 − cos 4x)/x² is
questions.why: 1 − cos 4x = 2 sin²2x, so (1 − cos 4x)/x² = 2 (sin 2x/x)² → 2 × 2² = 8.

questions.q: Assertion: lim (x→0) |x|/x does not exist. Reason: the left- and right-hand limits are unequal.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
Both true and R explains A
questions.why: Both are true. For x > 0, |x|/x = 1 and for x < 0 it is −1, so the left and right limits (−1 and 1) differ and the limit does not exist. The reason is exactly why the limit fails.

questions.q: lim (x→a) (√x − √a)/(x − a) for a > 0 is
questions.why: Using lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = n aⁿ⁻¹ with n = 1/2 gives (1/2)a⁻¹ᐟ² = 1/(2√a). Alternatively multiply by (√x + √a)/(√x + √a).

questions.q: d/dx [(x² + 1)(x − 3)] is
questions.why: Expand: (x² + 1)(x − 3) = x³ − 3x² + x − 3. Differentiating gives 3x² − 6x + 1.

questions.q: d/dx (x/(1 + x)) is
questions.why: By the quotient rule: [1·(1 + x) − x·1]/(1 + x)² = 1/(1 + x)².

questions.q: If f(x) = x¹⁰⁰ + x⁹⁹ + … + x + 1, then f′(1) is
Case: A balloon's volume is V = (4/3)πr³. The rate of change of V with respect to r at r = 3 cm is
questions.why: The rate of change of V with respect to r is dV/dr = 4πr². At r = 3 this is 4π × 9 = 36π cm³ per cm.

questions.q: lim (x→0) (sin ax + bx)/(ax + sin bx) for a, b, a + b ≠ 0 is
questions.why: Divide numerator and denominator by x: (sin ax/x + b)/(a + sin bx/x). As x → 0, sin ax/x → a and sin bx/x → b, giving (a + b)/(a + b) = 1.

questions.q: For f(x) = 5x − 4 for 0 < x ≤ 1 and 4x³ − 3x for 1 < x < 2, lim (x→1) f(x) is
questions.why: Left limit: 5(1) − 4 = 1. Right limit: 4(1)³ − 3(1) = 1. Both equal 1, so the limit is 1.

questions.q: d/dx (sec x) from rules: (1/cos x)′ =
questions.why: Using the chain/quotient rule, (1/cos x)′ = −(−sin x)/cos²x = sin x/cos²x = sec x tan x.

questions.q: If lim (x→1) (x⁴ − 1)/(x − 1) = lim (x→k) (x³ − k³)/(x² − k²), then k =
questions.why: The left side is 4 (derivative of x⁴ at 1). The right side is 3k²/(2k) = 3k/2. Setting 3k/2 = 4 gives k = 8/3.

questions.q: Derivative of (x + cos x)/tan x is
options: [(1 − sin x) tan x − (x + cos x) sec²x]/tan²x
[(1 + sin x) tan x − (x + cos x) sec²x]/tan²x
questions.why: By the quotient rule with u = x + cos x (u′ = 1 − sin x) and v = tan x (v′ = sec²x): (u′v − uv′)/v² = [(1 − sin x) tan x − (x + cos x) sec²x]/tan²x.

courses.title: Ch 13 · Statistics
courses.summary: Measures of dispersion: range, mean deviation about mean and median for ungrouped and grouped data, variance and standard deviation including the shortcut method, and comparing variability.
outcomes: Learners can explain why central tendency alone is not enough
Learners can compute range and mean deviation for ungrouped and grouped data
Learners can compute variance and standard deviation by direct and shortcut methods
Learners can compare two distributions using the coefficient of variation

scenes.text: Batsmen A and B both average 50. A scores 48, 50, 52; B scores 0, 50, 100.
Same mean, very different consistency. Measures of dispersion capture the spread.

steps.title: Measures of dispersion
steps.body:
- **Range** = maximum − minimum (simple but uses only two values).
- **Mean deviation about a**: M.D.(a) = Σ|xᵢ − a| / n. Usually a = mean x̄ or median M.
- Mean deviation is least when taken about the median.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the absolute value (Σ(xᵢ − x̄) is always 0).
- Finding the median without sorting.
- Dividing by n − 1 (Class 11 uses n).

activity.prompt: Find the mean deviation about the mean for 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.

quiz.q: Range of 12, 5, 19, 7, 3 is
quiz.why: Range = largest value − smallest value = 19 − 3 = 16.

quiz.q: Σ(xᵢ − x̄) for any data equals
quiz.why: The deviations from the mean add up to zero, since values above the mean cancel those below it. So Σ(xᵢ − x̄) = 0.

quiz.q: Mean deviation is smallest about the
quiz.why: The mean deviation is smallest when it is taken about the median. This is a known property of the median.

quiz.q: M.D. about the mean of 1, 1, 1, 1 is
quiz.why: All the values are equal, so every deviation from the mean is zero and the mean deviation is 0 (no spread).

quiz.q: Batsman with scores 0, 50, 100 is ___ than one with 48, 50, 52.
quiz.why: Scores 0, 50, 100 are widely spread while 48, 50, 52 are close together, though both average 50. A bigger spread means less consistency.

scenes.text: A survey records daily wages of 50 workers in class intervals.
We cannot see each value, so we use class marks to estimate the spread.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- Discrete frequency distribution: x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ/N, **M.D.(x̄) = Σfᵢ|xᵢ − x̄|/N** (N = Σfᵢ).
- About the median: find the median from cumulative frequencies, then Σfᵢ|xᵢ − M|/N.
- Continuous classes: use class marks xᵢ (midpoints). Median = l + [(N/2 − c.f.)/f] × h.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying |xᵢ − x̄| by fᵢ is required — not optional.
- Using class limits instead of class marks.
- Locating the median class with N instead of N/2.

items: Find class marks and cumulative frequencies
Locate the median class using N/2
Compute the median with l + [(N/2 − c.f.)/f] × h
Find |xᵢ − M| for each class mark
Divide Σfᵢ|xᵢ − M| by N

quiz.why: For grouped data, each class is represented by its class mark (midpoint), so deviations are measured from the class marks.

scenes.text: A bottling plant fills 500 ml bottles. Customers complain if some are 480 ml and others 520 ml.
Engineers track the standard deviation of fill volumes — the most widely used measure of spread.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Variance** σ² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/n; for frequencies σ² = Σfᵢ(xᵢ − x̄)²/N.
- **Standard deviation** σ = √variance (same units as the data).
- Computing form: σ² = Σxᵢ²/n − x̄².
- **Shortcut (step deviation):** yᵢ = (xᵢ − A)/h, then σₓ = h·σᵧ, with σᵧ² = Σfy²/N − (Σfy/N)².
- Adding a constant to all data does not change σ; multiplying by k multiplies σ by |k|.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking σ as the variance (forgetting the square root).
- In the shortcut, forgetting to multiply by h² for variance (or h for σ).
- Using (Σx)² instead of Σx².

quiz.why: Adding 10 to every observation shifts the whole data, but the gaps between values stay the same, so the standard deviation does not change.

B has the smaller σ, but relative to its price it swings more. We need a relative measure.

steps.title: Coefficient of variation
steps.body:
**C.V. = (σ / x̄) × 100**, a unitless percentage.
- The series with the **greater C.V.** is more variable; the smaller C.V. is more **consistent/stable**.
- With equal means, compare σ directly.

steps.title: Solved example 1: shares
steps.body:
C.V.(A) = 5/100 × 100 = 5%. C.V.(B) = 2/20 × 100 = 10%.

- **A is more stable**, even though its σ is larger.

steps.title: Solved example 2: two firms
steps.body:
Firm A: mean wage ₹5253, variance 100; Firm B: mean ₹5253, variance 121.

- Equal means → compare σ: 10 vs 11.
- Firm B has greater variability in individual wages.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing σ of data in different units or with very different means.
- Using the variance in the C.V. formula instead of σ.
- Saying the larger C.V. is 'more consistent' (it is the opposite).

Case: Two players' scores: A mean 40, σ 10; B mean 50, σ 15. Who is more consistent?
questions.why: C.V. of A = 10/40 × 100 = 25% and of B = 15/50 × 100 = 30%. A has the smaller C.V., so A is more consistent, even though B's mean is higher.

Case: Heights of 50 students have mean 160 cm and σ 5 cm; weights mean 50 kg, σ 4 kg. Which varies more relatively?
questions.why: Heights have C.V. = 5/160 × 100 = 3.125% and weights have C.V. = 4/50 × 100 = 8%. The C.V. is unitless, so the quantities can be compared: weight varies more relatively.

questions.why: With the shortcut method u = (x − A)/h, the data are scaled by h, so σₓ = h × σᵤ = 10 × 1.5 = 15.

questions.why: For the first n natural numbers variance = (n² − 1)/12. With n = 10, that is 99/12 = 8.25.

questions.why: The range uses only the two extreme values, while mean deviation uses every observation, so it describes the spread better.

scenes.text: Before every cricket match, the captains toss a coin. Nobody can predict the outcome, but everyone knows the possibilities.
Listing all possible outcomes is the first step in probability.

steps.title: Definitions
Solved example 1
steps.body:
A coin is tossed; if it shows head a die is thrown, otherwise the coin is tossed again.

- S = {H1, H2, H3, H4, H5, H6, TH, TT} → **8 outcomes**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Two balls are drawn one after another (without replacement) from a bag of 2 red (R₁, R₂) and 1 blue (B).

- S = {R₁R₂, R₁B, R₂R₁, R₂B, BR₁, BR₂} → 6 ordered outcomes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating HT and TH as the same when order matters.
- Forgetting outcomes in multi-stage experiments.
- Listing an event instead of the full sample space.

activity.prompt: How many outcomes are in the sample space when three coins are tossed?

quiz.q: Sample space for one die has
quiz.why: A die has six faces, so the sample space is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, i.e. 6 points.

quiz.q: Number of outcomes when 2 dice are thrown is
quiz.why: Each of the 6 outcomes on the first die pairs with 6 on the second, so there are 6 × 6 = 36 outcomes.

quiz.q: Which is a random experiment?
options: Drawing a card from a well-shuffled deck
quiz.why: A random experiment has outcomes that cannot be predicted in advance. Drawing a card from a shuffled deck qualifies, while the others have fixed results.

quiz.q: Sample space of tossing a coin 2 times contains
quiz.why: Tossing a coin twice gives ordered pairs: HH, HT, TH, TT. HT and TH are different outcomes.

quiz.q: A family with 2 children (B/G, order by birth) has sample space of size
quiz.why: Each child can be a boy or a girl, and birth order matters, so the outcomes are BB, BG, GB, GG: 4 in all.

lessons.title: Events and the algebra of events

scenes.text: In a board game, you move if you roll an even number, and get a bonus if you roll more than 4.
'Even' and 'more than 4' are events — subsets of the sample space — and we can combine them.

steps.title: Events
steps.body:
An **event** is a subset of S. It *occurs* if the outcome is in it.
- **Impossible event** φ; **sure event** S; **simple event** (one point); **compound event** (more than one).
- **Not A** = A′ = S − A; **A or B** = A ∪ B; **A and B** = A ∩ B; **A but not B** = A − B = A ∩ B′.
- **Mutually exclusive:** A ∩ B = φ.
- **Exhaustive:** E₁ ∪ E₂ ∪ … ∪ Eₙ = S. If also pairwise disjoint, they are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Die thrown: A = even = {2, 4, 6}, B = more than 4 = {5, 6}.

- A ∪ B = {2, 4, 5, 6}; A ∩ B = {6}; A − B = {2, 4}; A′ = {1, 3, 5}.
- A and B are **not** mutually exclusive (6 is common).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Die: E₁ = {1, 2}, E₂ = {3, 4}, E₃ = {5, 6}.

- Pairwise disjoint and union is S → **mutually exclusive and exhaustive**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking an event and its complement can both occur — they are mutually exclusive.
- Confusing 'mutually exclusive' with 'exhaustive'.
- Writing 'A but not B' as B − A.

activity.prompt: Match the description with the set.

quiz.q: Events A and A′ are
quiz.why: An event A and its complement A′ share no outcomes (mutually exclusive) and together cover the whole sample space (exhaustive).

quiz.q: When two coins are tossed, 'at least one head' is
quiz.why: 'At least one head' includes HH, HT and TH. Only TT has no head, so it is left out.

quiz.q: On a die, 'a number greater than 6' is
quiz.why: A die has only faces 1 to 6, so 'a number greater than 6' can never happen. It is an impossible event, with probability 0.
A ∩ B is the set of elements common to both. Only 3 is in both {1, 3, 5} and {2, 3}.
A and B share no element (mutually exclusive), and A ∪ B = {1, …, 6} is the whole sample space (exhaustive).

scenes.text: An app says 70% chance of rain. Could it say 120%? Could rain and no rain add to 90%?
No — probability obeys three simple axioms that keep it sensible.

steps.title: The axioms
steps.body:
A probability function P on events of S satisfies:
- (i) P(E) ≥ 0 for every event E
- (ii) P(S) = 1
- (iii) If E and F are mutually exclusive, P(E ∪ F) = P(E) + P(F)

Consequences: P(φ) = 0; 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1; P(E) = sum of probabilities of its sample points.

**Equally likely outcomes:** if S has n equally likely points, **P(E) = n(E)/n(S)**.

steps.title: Solved example 1: valid assignment?
steps.body: S = {ω₁, ω₂, ω₃} with P = 0.5, 0.3, 0.2. Valid: each ≥ 0 and sum 1. With P = 0.6, 0.6, −0.2 it is **not valid** (negative value).

steps.title: Solved example 2: dice
steps.body:
Two dice: probability that the sum is 8.

- Favourable: (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2) → 5.
- P = **5/36**.

steps.title: Solved example 3: cards
steps.body:
A card is drawn from a 52-card deck. P(a king or a heart)?

- Kings 4, hearts 13, king of hearts counted twice: 4 + 13 − 1 = 16.
- P = 16/52 = **4/13**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming outcomes are equally likely when they are not (e.g. sums of two dice).
- Probabilities outside [0, 1] — always a sign of an error.
- Counting the overlap twice.

activity.prompt: Two dice are thrown. What is the probability (as a decimal to 3 places) that the sum is 7?

quiz.q: P(S) equals
quiz.why: The probability of the whole sample space is 1, since some outcome in S is certain to occur.

quiz.q: Probability of a head on a fair coin is
quiz.why: A fair coin has 2 equally likely outcomes and one is a head, so P(head) = 1/2.

quiz.q: Probability of drawing an ace from a deck is
quiz.why: A deck has 4 aces out of 52 cards, so P = 4/52 = 1/13.

quiz.q: Which can be a probability?
quiz.why: A probability must lie between 0 and 1. Only 0.75 does; 3/2, 1.2 and −0.1 fall outside that range.

quiz.q: Probability of getting a prime on a die is
quiz.why: The prime numbers on a die are 2, 3 and 5, i.e. 3 favourable outcomes of 6, so P = 3/6 = 1/2. (1 is not prime.)

scenes.text: A school lottery picks 4 winners from 20 tickets. Aman holds 2 tickets.
Combining combinations with probability rules tells him his real chances.

steps.title: Key rules
steps.body:
- **P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)**
- If A, B mutually exclusive: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B)
- **P(A′) = 1 − P(A)**
- P(A − B) = P(A) − P(A ∩ B)
- 'At least one' = 1 − P(none)
- With counting: P = (favourable selections)/(total selections), often using ⁿCᵣ.

steps.title: Solved example 2: committee
steps.body:
A committee of 2 is chosen from 2 men and 2 women. P(at least one woman)?

- Total ⁴C₂ = 6; no woman = 1 (both men).
- P = 1 − 1/6 = **5/6**.

steps.title: Solved example 3: cards
steps.body: 4 cards from a deck: P(all four are diamonds) = ¹³C₄/⁵²C₄ = 715/270725 ≈ **0.0026**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding probabilities of events that overlap without subtracting the intersection.
- Using permutations in numerator and combinations in denominator (mixing).
- For 'at least one', counting cases one by one and double-counting.

activity.prompt: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.3 and A, B are mutually exclusive. Find P(neither A nor B).

quiz.q: If P(A) = 0.35, then P(not A) is

quiz.why: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) = 0.6 + 0.5 − 0.3 = 0.8. The overlap must be subtracted so it is not counted twice.

quiz.q: P(at least one head in 3 tosses) is
quiz.why: The only outcome with no heads is TTT, with probability 1/8. So P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8.

quiz.q: A letter is chosen from 'ASSASSINATION'. P(vowel) is
quiz.why: ASSASSINATION has 13 letters, and the vowels are A (3 times), I (2 times) and O (1 time), 6 in all. So P(vowel) = 6/13.

quiz.q: For mutually exclusive A, B with P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 1/3, P(A ∪ B) =
quiz.why: For mutually exclusive events there is no overlap, so P(A ∪ B) = 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6.

questions.q: Number of sample points when a die is rolled twice is
questions.why: Each roll has 6 outcomes, and two rolls give 6 × 6 = 36 sample points.

questions.q: Probability of an impossible event is
questions.why: An impossible event contains no outcomes, so its probability is 0.

questions.q: If P(E) = 0.05, P(not E) is
questions.why: The probability of the complement is 1 − P(E) = 1 − 0.05 = 0.95.

questions.q: Probability of a sum of 12 with two dice is
questions.why: The sum 12 needs a 6 on both dice, which is only (6, 6). So the probability is 1/36.

questions.q: A card is drawn. P(red face card) is
questions.why: Red face cards are the J, Q, K of hearts and of diamonds: 6 cards. So P = 6/52 = 3/26.

questions.q: Events A, B with P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∪ B) = 0.7 are
questions.why: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∪ B) = 0.5 + 0.4 − 0.7 = 0.2, which is not zero. So the events can happen together and are not mutually exclusive.

questions.q: Assertion: P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.7 cannot be mutually exclusive. Reason: then P(A ∪ B) would be 1.3 > 1.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. If A and B were mutually exclusive, P(A ∪ B) = 0.6 + 0.7 = 1.3, which exceeds 1 and is impossible. So that is why they cannot be mutually exclusive.

questions.q: Three coins are tossed. P(exactly two heads) is
questions.why: Of the 8 equally likely outcomes, exactly two heads occur in HHT, HTH and THH. So P = 3/8.

questions.q: If A and B are events with P(A ∪ B) = 0.6 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.2, then P(A′) + P(B′) =
Case: In a class, 40% study Maths, 30% Biology and 10% both. P(a random student studies Maths or Biology) is
questions.why: P(Maths or Biology) = 0.4 + 0.3 − 0.1 = 0.6. The 0.1 who take both would otherwise be counted twice.

questions.q: Case: For the same class, P(neither subject) is
questions.why: P(neither subject) = 1 − P(Maths or Biology) = 1 − 0.6 = 0.4.

questions.q: A bag has 9 discs: 4 red, 3 blue, 2 yellow. P(not blue) for one random disc is
questions.why: There are 9 − 3 = 6 discs that are not blue, so P(not blue) = 6/9 = 2/3. (Equivalently 1 − 3/9.)

questions.q: From 6 employees, 2 are chosen at random. If 2 of the 6 are a married couple, P(the chosen pair is that couple) is
questions.why: Choosing 2 of 6 employees gives ⁶C₂ = 15 equally likely pairs. Only one of them is the couple, so P = 1/15.

questions.q: 5 cards are drawn from a deck. P(all are spades) is
questions.why: The number of favourable 5-card hands is ¹³C₅ (all from the 13 spades), out of ⁵²C₅ total hands. So P = ¹³C₅/⁵²C₅.

questions.q: A 4-digit number is formed with the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 without repetition. P(it is divisible by 5) is
questions.why: A number divisible by 5 must end in 5. The other 3 places use the remaining 4 digits in ⁴P₃ = 24 ways, out of ⁵P₄ = 120 total. So P = 24/120 = 1/5.

questions.q: In a lottery, a person chooses 6 different numbers from 1 to 20. P(winning, i.e. matching the 6 drawn numbers) is
questions.why: There are ²⁰C₆ = 38760 equally likely sets of 6 numbers, and only one wins, so P = 1/38760.

questions.q: If P(A) = 3/5 and P(B) = 1/5 with A, B mutually exclusive, P(A′ ∩ B′) is
questions.why: A and B are mutually exclusive, so P(A ∪ B) = 3/5 + 1/5 = 4/5. A′ ∩ B′ is 'neither', whose probability is 1 − 4/5 = 1/5.

lessons.title: Formula sheet I: Algebra (Ch 1–8)

scenes.text: It is the night before the half-yearly exam. Pooja has no time to reread 8 chapters.
One clean formula sheet, read twice and tested once, is her best friend.

steps.title: Sets, relations, functions
steps.body:
- n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B); De Morgan: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′
- n(P(A)) = 2ⁿ; proper subsets 2ⁿ − 1
- n(A × B) = pq; relations A → B: 2^(pq)
- [x], |x|, sgn x: know their graphs, domains and ranges

steps.title: Trigonometry
steps.body:
- π rad = 180°, l = rθ
- sin(x ± y), cos(x ± y) = cos x cos y ∓ sin x sin y, tan(x ± y)
- sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x; cos 2x = 1 − 2sin²x = 2cos²x − 1; tan 2x = 2tan x/(1 − tan²x)
- sin 3x = 3 sin x − 4 sin³x; cos 3x = 4cos³x − 3cos x
- sin C + sin D = 2 sin((C+D)/2) cos((C−D)/2), etc.

steps.title: Complex numbers, inequalities, P&C
steps.body:
- i² = −1, iⁿ cycles every 4; |z| = √(a² + b²), z z̄ = |z|², z⁻¹ = z̄/|z|²
- Polar: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ)
- D < 0: x = (−b ± i√(4ac − b²))/2a
- Inequalities: multiply by negative → flip
- ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!; ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!); ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ; ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₋₁ = ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ; identical objects n!/(p!q!…)

steps.title: Binomial, sequences
steps.body:
- Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ; ΣⁿCᵣ = 2ⁿ
- A.P.: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d, Sₙ = (n/2)(2a + (n − 1)d)
- G.P.: aₙ = arⁿ⁻¹, Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1), S∞ = a/(1 − r) (|r| < 1)
- A.M. ≥ G.M.; Σk = n(n + 1)/2, Σk² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6, Σk³ = [n(n + 1)/2]²

steps.title: Top errors to avoid
steps.body:
- Sign of trigonometric functions by quadrant
- Forgetting n + 1 terms in a binomial expansion
- Using P instead of C when order does not matter
- √(−a)√(−b) ≠ √(ab)

quiz.q: cos 2x in terms of sin x is
quiz.why: cos 2x = cos²x − sin²x, and replacing cos²x with 1 − sin²x gives 1 − 2 sin²x.

quiz.q: Number of terms in (a + b)²⁰ is
quiz.why: (a + b)ⁿ has n + 1 terms, so (a + b)²⁰ has 21 terms.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Mathematics (Revision & Practice · Class 11 Mathematics)

lessons.title: Formula sheet II: Geometry, calculus, statistics, probability (Ch 9–14)

scenes.text: Arjun folds a single A4 sheet into six boxes — one per chapter — and fills each with what he must never forget.
Writing the sheet himself is itself the best revision.

steps.title: Straight lines and conics
steps.body:
- m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁); ∥: m₁ = m₂; ⟂: m₁m₂ = −1; tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)|
- y − y₁ = m(x − x₁); y = mx + c; x/a + y/b = 1
- d = |Ax₁ + By₁ + C|/√(A² + B²); parallel lines |C₁ − C₂|/√(A² + B²)
- Circle centre (−g, −f), r = √(g² + f² − c)
- Parabola y² = 4ax: focus (a, 0), directrix x = −a, LR 4a
- Ellipse: c² = a² − b², e = c/a < 1, LR 2b²/a; Hyperbola: c² = a² + b², e > 1, LR 2b²/a

steps.title: 3D geometry, limits, derivatives
steps.body:
- PQ = √(Δx² + Δy² + Δz²); octant signs
- lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹; lim sin x/x = 1; lim (1 − cos x)/x = 0
- f′(x) = lim [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h
- (uv)′ = u′v + uv′; (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²
- sin → cos, cos → −sin, tan → sec², sec → sec tan, cot → −cosec², cosec → −cosec cot

steps.title: Statistics and probability
steps.body:
- M.D. = Σf|x − a|/N; σ² = Σf(x − x̄)²/N = Σfx²/N − x̄²; σₓ = h σᵧ
- C.V. = σ/x̄ × 100
- P(E) = n(E)/n(S); P(A′) = 1 − P(A); P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

steps.title: Mixed solved example
steps.body:
Find the equation of the circle whose centre is the focus of y² = 8x and which passes through the vertex.

- Focus (2, 0); vertex (0, 0); r = 2.
- (x − 2)² + y² = 4 → **x² + y² − 4x = 0**.

steps.title: Top errors to avoid
steps.body:
- Ellipse vs hyperbola c-formula mix-up
- Forgetting the modulus in distance formulas
- Degrees in sin x/x limits
- Forgetting to take √ for σ

pairs: Distance from a point to a line

quiz.q: Latus rectum of y² = 4ax is
quiz.why: For the parabola y² = 4ax, the length of the latus rectum is 4a, the chord through the focus perpendicular to the axis.

quiz.q: d/dx (cot x) is
quiz.why: The standard result is d/dx (cot x) = −cosec²x. The derivative of tan x is the one with sec².

quiz.q: lim (x→0) tan 3x / x is
quiz.why: Write tan 3x/x = 3 · (tan 3x/3x). Since tan u/u → 1 as u → 0, the limit is 3.

quiz.q: P(A ∪ B) for mutually exclusive A, B is
quiz.why: Mutually exclusive events have no overlap, so their probabilities simply add: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B).

quiz.q: Slope of a line perpendicular to slope 3/4 is
quiz.why: Perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is −1. So the slope is −1/(3/4) = −4/3.

lessons.title: Exam strategy and mixed practice

scenes.text: Kunal always ran out of time in maths papers — he got stuck on question 5 for 25 minutes.
This time he reads the whole paper first, does sure-shot questions, marks the hard ones and comes back. He finishes with 15 minutes to check.

steps.title: Before the exam
steps.body:
- Revise from your formula sheet and one solved example per topic.
- Re-solve your past mistakes — they repeat.
- Sleep well; tired brains make sign errors.

steps.title: In the exam
steps.body:
- First 10 minutes: read everything, tick easy questions.
- Show steps — marks are given for method.
- Box final answers with units.
- If stuck for 3–4 minutes, move on and return later.
- Keep 10–15 minutes to check signs, brackets and arithmetic.

steps.title: Mixed problem 1
steps.body:
If tan x = −4/3 with x in QII, find sin(x/2).

- cos x = −3/5. sin²(x/2) = (1 − cos x)/2 = (1 + 3/5)/2 = 4/5.
- x/2 lies in QI (π/4 < x/2 < π/2), so sin(x/2) = **2/√5**.

steps.title: Mixed problem 2
steps.body:
How many terms of the A.P. −6, −11/2, −5, … sum to −25?

- a = −6, d = 1/2: (n/2)[−12 + (n − 1)/2] = −25 → n² − 25n + 100 = 0 → n = 5 or 20.
- Both are valid (the terms from 6th to 20th sum to 0).

steps.title: Self-check list
steps.body:
- Did I answer what was asked (term vs coefficient, P vs C)?
- Did I include the domain restrictions?
- Is a probability between 0 and 1? Is a length positive?

activity.prompt: Exam-readiness checklist
items: I made my own one-page formula sheet
I solved one mock paper in 3 hours without notes
I listed my 10 most common mistakes
I can derive sin 15°, sin 3x and the 3D distance formula
I practised 5 limit and 5 derivative questions today
I know what to do when I get stuck

quiz.q: When stuck on a question for several minutes, you should
quiz.why: If you are stuck, move on and come back later, so you do not lose time for questions you can solve. Guessing and never returning, or leaving, wastes marks.

quiz.q: Marks in board exams are often given for
quiz.why: Board examiners award marks for each correct step of the method, so showing working earns marks even if the final answer slips.

quiz.q: A probability answer of 1.2 indicates
quiz.why: A probability must be between 0 and 1, so a value of 1.2 means a mistake has been made somewhere in the working.

quiz.q: If tan x = −4/3 in QII, cos x is
quiz.why: tan x = −4/3 with x in the second quadrant gives a 3-4-5 triangle. There cosine is negative, so cos x = −3/5.

quiz.q: The best revision of formulas is to
options: write them yourself and test yourself
quiz.why: Writing formulas yourself and testing yourself is active recall, which builds memory better than just reading or memorising without practice.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q2. Domain of f(x) = 1/(x − 5) is
questions.why: The function 1/(x − 5) is undefined when x − 5 = 0, i.e. x = 5. So the domain is all real numbers except 5.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q3. sin 120° equals
questions.why: sin 120° = sin(180° − 60°) = sin 60° = √3/2. Sine is positive in the second quadrant.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q4. (1 + i)/(1 − i) equals
Mock 1 · Q5. Solution of 3 − 2x ≤ 9 is
questions.why: 3 − 2x ≤ 9 gives −2x ≤ 6. Dividing by −2 reverses the inequality, so x ≥ −3.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q6. Number of ways to arrange the letters of 'LEVEL' is
questions.why: LEVEL has 5 letters with L twice and E twice. Arrangements = 5!/(2! 2!) = 120/4 = 30.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q7. Coefficient of x⁴ in (1 + 2x)⁶ is
questions.why: The x⁴ term is ⁶C₄(2x)⁴ = 15 × 16x⁴ = 240x⁴, so the coefficient is 240.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q8. The sum of the infinite G.P. 6 + 2 + 2/3 + … is
questions.why: This is a G.P. with a = 6 and r = 1/3, so the sum to infinity is 6/(1 − 1/3) = 6/(2/3) = 9.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q9. If 3 tan x = 4 with x acute, sin 2x =
questions.why: 3 tan x = 4 gives tan x = 4/3, a 3-4-5 triangle, so sin x = 4/5 and cos x = 3/5. Then sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x = 2 × 4/5 × 3/5 = 24/25.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q10. The number of 5-card hands with at least one ace from a 52-card deck is
questions.why: Hands with at least one ace = all hands − hands with no ace = ⁵²C₅ − ⁴⁸C₅. The other options undercount or count every hand.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q1. Slope of 4x − 2y + 7 = 0 is
questions.why: The slope of Ax + By + C = 0 is −A/B = −4/(−2) = 2.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q2. Centre of x² + y² − 10x + 4y − 7 = 0 is
questions.why: For x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 the centre is (−g, −f). Here 2g = −10 and 2f = 4, so g = −5, f = 2 and the centre is (5, −2).

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q3. d/dx (x³ sin x) is
questions.why: By the product rule, d/dx (x³ sin x) = 3x² sin x + x³ cos x.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q4. lim (x→0) sin 7x / 2x is
questions.why: sin 7x/2x = (7/2)(sin 7x/7x). Since sin u/u → 1, the limit is 7/2.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q5. Distance between (1, −2, 3) and (3, 0, 4) is
Mock 2 · Q6. Eccentricity of x²/9 + y²/5 = 1 is
questions.why: For x²/9 + y²/5 = 1, a² = 9 and b² = 5, so c² = 9 − 5 = 4 and c = 2. Eccentricity e = c/a = 2/3.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q7. Variance of 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 is
questions.why: The mean is 6. Squared deviations are 16, 4, 0, 4, 16, which sum to 40. Variance = 40/5 = 8.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q8. Two dice are thrown. P(doublet) is
questions.why: A doublet means both dice show the same number: (1,1), …, (6,6), which is 6 of the 36 outcomes. P = 6/36 = 1/6.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q9. Equation of the parabola with focus (0, 4) and directrix y = −4 is
questions.why: A focus (0, a) with a directrix y = −a gives a = 4, and the parabola opens upward: x² = 4ay = 16y.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q10. The derivative of (sin x + cos x)/(sin x − cos x) is
questions.why: Numerator: (cos − sin)(sin − cos) − (sin + cos)(cos + sin) = −(sin − cos)² − (sin + cos)² = −2.

school-c11-physics-a.title: Class 11 Physics · Part A (Ch 1–4)
school-c11-physics-a.description: Class 11 Physics chapter by chapter: Units and Measurement, Motion in a Straight Line, Motion in a Plane and Laws of Motion — derivations, solved numericals and JEE/NEET bridge practice.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Units and Measurement
courses.summary: SI units, significant figures, errors and their propagation, and dimensional analysis — the toolkit every later chapter uses.
outcomes: Learners can name the seven SI base quantities and units and build derived units
Learners can apply significant-figure and rounding rules in calculations
Learners can compute absolute, relative and percentage errors and combine them
Learners can use dimensions to check equations and derive simple relations

lessons.title: SI units, base and derived quantities

scenes.text: Riya's father drives at 72 km/h. Her physics sheet asks for speed in m/s.
She realises every formula in physics expects SI units — so she learns to convert before calculating.

steps.title: Base quantities and units
steps.body:
The SI system has **seven base quantities**:
- length — metre (m)
- mass — kilogram (kg)
- time — second (s)
- electric current — ampere (A)
- thermodynamic temperature — kelvin (K)
- amount of substance — mole (mol)
- luminous intensity — candela (cd)

Two supplementary units are used for angles: radian (rad) for plane angle and steradian (sr) for solid angle. Every other unit is **derived** from base units, e.g. force: kg m s⁻² = newton (N); energy: kg m² s⁻² = joule (J).

steps.title: Prefixes you must know
steps.body:
- kilo (k) 10³, mega (M) 10⁶, giga (G) 10⁹
- centi (c) 10⁻², milli (m) 10⁻³, micro (µ) 10⁻⁶, nano (n) 10⁻⁹, pico (p) 10⁻¹², femto (f) 10⁻¹⁵

Useful non-SI length units: 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m, 1 fermi = 10⁻¹⁵ m, 1 light year ≈ 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m, 1 AU ≈ 1.496 × 10¹¹ m, 1 parsec ≈ 3.08 × 10¹⁶ m.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Convert 72 km/h to m/s.
- 1 km = 1000 m, 1 h = 3600 s
- 72 × 1000 / 3600 = 20 m/s
- Shortcut: multiply km/h by 5/18.

**Example 2:** Density of water is 1 g/cm³. Express in kg/m³.
- 1 g = 10⁻³ kg; 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³
- 1 × 10⁻³ / 10⁻⁶ = 10³ kg/m³ = 1000 kg/m³

**Example 3:** Express 1 N in CGS (dyne).
- 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻² = 10³ g × 10² cm s⁻² = 10⁵ dyne

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing units as plurals or with full stops: write 5 kg, not 5 kgs or 5 kg.
- Mixing CGS and SI inside one formula.
- Converting area or volume with the linear factor: 1 m² = 10⁴ cm², not 10² cm².
- Confusing mass (kg) with weight (N).

activity.prompt: Match each quantity to its SI unit

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT an SI base unit?
quiz.why: The newton is a derived unit (kg·m·s⁻²). The candela, kelvin and mole are SI base units.

quiz.q: 36 km/h equals
quiz.why: To convert km/h to m/s multiply by 5/18: 36 × 5/18 = 10 m/s.

quiz.q: 1 light year is a unit of
quiz.why: A light year is the distance light travels in one year, so despite 'year' it measures distance, not time.

quiz.q: How many cm³ are there in 1 m³?
quiz.why: 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m³ = (100 cm)³ = 10⁶ cm³. Cubing the length factor gives the volume factor.

quiz.q: The SI unit of solid angle is
quiz.why: The steradian (sr) is the SI unit of solid angle. The radian is for plane angle.

scenes.text: Arjun writes the length as 2.5 cm and the width as 3.42 cm, then reports area as 8.55 cm².
His teacher asks: can a product be more precise than the least precise measurement? Arjun corrects it to 8.6 cm².

steps.title: Rules for counting significant figures
steps.body:
- All non-zero digits are significant.
- Zeros between non-zero digits are significant (2005 has 4).
- Leading zeros are NOT significant (0.0045 has 2).
- Trailing zeros after a decimal point ARE significant (4.500 has 4).
- Trailing zeros in a whole number without a decimal point are ambiguous — use scientific notation: 4.50 × 10³ has 3.
- Exact numbers (counted items, defined constants like 2 in 2πr) have infinite significant figures.

steps.title: Arithmetic rules
steps.body:
**Multiplication/division:** the result keeps as many significant figures as the factor with the fewest significant figures.

**Addition/subtraction:** the result keeps as many decimal places as the term with the fewest decimal places.

**Rounding:** if the dropped digit is more than 5, round up; less than 5, leave; exactly 5 (followed by nothing), make the preceding digit even (2.745 → 2.74, 2.735 → 2.74).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** How many significant figures in 0.007020?
- Leading zeros 0.00 are not significant.
- 7, 0, 2 and the trailing 0 after the decimal are significant → **4**.

**Example 2:** 2.5 cm × 3.42 cm = ?
- Raw product 8.55; least s.f. = 2 (in 2.5)
- Answer **8.6 cm²**

**Example 3:** 12.11 + 18.0 + 1.013 = ?
- Raw sum 31.123; fewest decimal places = 1 (18.0)
- Answer **31.1**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rounding at every intermediate step — keep one extra digit and round only at the end.
- Counting leading zeros as significant.
- Applying the decimal-place rule to multiplication.
- Changing units changes s.f.? No: 2.30 m = 230 cm keeps 3 s.f. — write 2.30 × 10² cm to show it.

activity.prompt: Sort each number by its count of significant figures

quiz.q: Number of significant figures in 6.320 × 10⁴ is
quiz.why: In 6.320 × 10⁴, the digits 6, 3, 2 and the trailing 0 after the decimal point are all significant, giving 4 significant figures.

quiz.q: 4.0 × 2.123 should be reported as
quiz.why: In multiplication the answer has as many significant figures as the least precise number. 4.0 has 2, so 4.0 × 2.123 = 8.492 is rounded to 8.5.
In addition the result keeps the fewest decimal places of the numbers added. 3.5 has one decimal, so 4.861 is rounded to 4.9.

quiz.q: Rounded to 3 s.f., 2.745 becomes
quiz.why: When the digit to be dropped is exactly 5, the usual rule is to keep the preceding digit if it is even. Since the preceding digit 4 is even, 2.745 becomes 2.74.

quiz.q: The 2 in the formula C = 2πr has how many significant figures?
quiz.why: The 2 in C = 2πr is an exact number from the definition, so it has unlimited significant figures and does not limit the precision of the answer.

scenes.text: Five students time one pendulum swing and get slightly different values.
Instead of arguing, they compute the mean and the mean absolute error — and report the period as a value ± error.

steps.title: Types of error
steps.body:
- **Systematic errors** push results in one direction: instrumental (zero error), imperfect technique, personal bias. Reduced by better method and calibration.
- **Random errors** vary unpredictably; reduced by taking many readings and averaging.
- **Least count error** is the resolution of the instrument (e.g. vernier 0.01 cm, screw gauge 0.001 cm).

steps.title: Absolute, relative and percentage error
steps.body:
For readings a₁, a₂ … aₙ:
- Mean a = (Σaᵢ)/n
- Absolute error Δaᵢ = aᵢ − a
- Mean absolute error Δa = (Σ|Δaᵢ|)/n
- Relative error = Δa / a; Percentage error = (Δa / a) × 100%

**Combination rules:**
- Z = A ± B → ΔZ = ΔA + ΔB (absolute errors add)
- Z = AB or A/B → ΔZ/Z = ΔA/A + ΔB/B (relative errors add)
- Z = Aᵖ Bᑫ / Cʳ → ΔZ/Z = pΔA/A + qΔB/B + rΔC/C

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Subtracting errors when quantities are subtracted — errors always ADD.
- Forgetting to multiply by the power (a squared term doubles its relative error).
- Reporting more decimals in the error than the measurement supports.
- Ignoring zero error of the instrument.

activity.prompt: Length l = (20.0 ± 0.1) cm and breadth b = (10.0 ± 0.1) cm. What is the percentage error in the area l × b?

quiz.q: If x = a³/b² and errors in a and b are 1% and 2%, the % error in x is
quiz.why: For x = a³/b², the percentage errors multiply by the powers and add: 3 × 1% + 2 × 2% = 7%. Errors add, even for division.

quiz.q: Random errors are reduced by
quiz.why: Random errors vary unpredictably, so taking many readings and averaging reduces their effect. Calibration fixes systematic errors instead.

quiz.q: For Z = A − B, ΔZ equals
quiz.why: For both addition and subtraction the maximum absolute errors add: ΔZ = ΔA + ΔB. The errors never cancel in the worst case.

quiz.q: A zero error in a screw gauge is a
options: gross error that cannot be corrected
quiz.why: A zero error shifts every reading in the same direction by the same amount, so it is a systematic error, and it can be corrected by subtracting it.

quiz.q: Mean of 1.2, 1.4, 1.3 is 1.3. Mean absolute error is
quiz.why: The deviations from the mean 1.3 are 0.1, 0.1 and 0. The mean absolute error is (0.1 + 0.1 + 0)/3 ≈ 0.067.

story.title: Checking a formula without a textbook

scenes.text: Kabir half-remembers that a pendulum's period is T = 2π√(g/l). Something feels wrong.
He checks dimensions: √(g/l) has unit s⁻¹, not s. So it must be √(l/g). Dimensions caught the slip.

steps.title: Dimensions
steps.body:
The dimensions of a quantity show how it depends on base quantities, written with [M], [L], [T], [A], [K], [mol], [cd].
- Velocity [L T⁻¹]; acceleration [L T⁻²]
- Force [M L T⁻²]; work/energy [M L² T⁻²]
- Power [M L² T⁻³]; pressure [M L⁻¹ T⁻²]
- Gravitational constant G: [M⁻¹ L³ T⁻²]
- Angle, strain, refractive index: dimensionless [M⁰ L⁰ T⁰]

steps.title: Principle of homogeneity and uses
steps.body:
Only quantities with the same dimensions can be added, subtracted or equated. Uses:
- **Checking** correctness of an equation (necessary, not sufficient).
- **Converting** units between systems.
- **Deducing** relations among quantities (when the dependence is a product of powers).

**Limitations:** cannot find dimensionless constants (like 2π), cannot handle sums of terms or trigonometric/exponential functions, cannot tell scalars from vectors.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Check v² = u² + 2as.
- LHS [L² T⁻²]; u² [L² T⁻²]; as = [L T⁻²][L] = [L² T⁻²] → consistent.

**Example 2:** Derive T for a pendulum depending on l, m, g: T = k lᵃ mᵇ gᶜ.
- [T] = [L]ᵃ [M]ᵇ [L T⁻²]ᶜ
- M: b = 0; T: −2c = 1 → c = −½; L: a + c = 0 → a = ½
- T = k√(l/g) (experiment gives k = 2π)

**Example 3:** Is ½mv² = mgh dimensionally correct? Both sides [M L² T⁻²] → yes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a dimensionally correct equation must be physically correct (E = mv² is dimensionally fine but wrong by ½).
- Forgetting that arguments of sin, log and exp must be dimensionless.
- Mixing up dimensions of work and torque — both [M L² T⁻²] but different physical meaning.
- Treating radian as having dimensions.

activity.prompt: Match each quantity to its dimensional formula

quiz.q: Dimensions of impulse are the same as those of
quiz.why: Impulse = force × time = change in momentum, so its dimensions are [M L T⁻¹], same as momentum.

quiz.q: Which pair has identical dimensions?
quiz.why: Both work and torque have dimensions [M L² T⁻²], even though they are different physical quantities.

quiz.q: Dimensional analysis cannot determine
options: the value of a dimensionless constant
quiz.why: Dimensional analysis cannot find pure numbers such as ½ or 2π, because they have no dimensions. It can still check consistency and unit conversions.

quiz.q: In x = A sin(ωt), the dimension of ω is
quiz.why: The argument of a sine must be dimensionless, so ωt has no dimensions. Since t is [T], ω is [T⁻¹].

quiz.q: Dimensional formula of surface tension (force per length) is
quiz.why: Surface tension is force per unit length: [M L T⁻²]/[L] = [M T⁻²].

questions.q: The SI unit of luminous intensity is
questions.why: The candela (cd) is the SI base unit of luminous intensity. The lumen and lux are derived units.

questions.q: 1 fermi equals
questions.why: The fermi, used for nuclear sizes, equals 10⁻¹⁵ m (also called a femtometre).

questions.q: Number of significant figures in 0.06900 is
questions.why: Leading zeros are not significant, but the trailing zeros after the decimal point are. So 0.06900 has 4 significant figures: 6, 9, 0, 0.

questions.q: 108 km/h in m/s is
questions.why: Multiply km/h by 5/18 to get m/s: 108 × 5/18 = 30 m/s.

questions.q: Dimensions of power are
questions.why: Power is energy per unit time: [M L² T⁻²]/[T] = [M L² T⁻³].

questions.q: Assertion: A dimensionally correct equation may be wrong. Reason: Dimensional analysis cannot find numerical constants.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. An equation can have matching dimensions but still be wrong, for example if a numerical constant like ½ is missing, which dimensions cannot detect.

questions.q: 5.74 g occupies 1.2 cm³. Density with correct significant figures is
questions.why: Density = 5.74/1.2 = 4.783 g/cm³. The volume 1.2 has only 2 significant figures, so the answer is rounded to 4.8 g/cm³.

questions.q: If P = a³b²/(cd) with % errors 1, 2, 3, 4 in a, b, c, d, the % error in P is
questions.why: For P = a³b²/(cd), percentage error = 3(1) + 2(2) + 3 + 4 = 3 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 14%. All the errors add up.

questions.q: Which has the same dimensions as pressure?
questions.why: Energy per unit volume is J/m³ = N·m/m³ = N/m², which is the same as pressure.

questions.q: Case: A student measures a sphere's radius as (2.0 ± 0.1) cm. What is the percentage error in its volume?
questions.why: Since V ∝ r³, the percentage error in V is 3 times that in r. The error in r is 0.1/2.0 × 100 = 5%, so V has 3 × 5 = 15%.

questions.q: Using dimensions, the speed v of a wave on a string depending on tension F and mass per length µ is
questions.why: Tension has [M L T⁻²] and mass per length has [M L⁻¹], so F/μ has [L² T⁻²]. Taking the square root gives [L T⁻¹], which is speed: v = √(F/μ).

questions.q: Value of G is 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². In CGS (dyne cm² g⁻²) it is
questions.why: 1 N = 10⁵ dyne, 1 m² = 10⁴ cm², and 1 kg⁻² = (10³ g)⁻² = 10⁻⁶ g⁻². The net factor is 10⁵ × 10⁴ × 10⁻⁶ = 10³, so G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 10³ = 6.67 × 10⁻⁸.

questions.q: Readings of a length: 1.22, 1.24, 1.20, 1.26 cm. Mean absolute error is
questions.why: The mean is 1.23 cm. The deviations are 0.01, 0.01, 0.03, 0.03, and their average is 0.08/4 = 0.02 cm.

questions.q: In the relation y = a sin(bt − cx), dimensions of b/c are those of
questions.why: In sin(bt − cx), bt and cx are dimensionless, so b is [T⁻¹] and c is [L⁻¹]. Then b/c has dimensions [L T⁻¹], that of velocity.

questions.q: Which measurement is most precise?
questions.why: The last digit of 5.00 mm is the hundredths of a millimetre, so its uncertainty (about 0.01 mm) is the smallest of the options. The other values have larger absolute uncertainty.

questions.q: A physical quantity X = M L² T⁻² could be
questions.why: [M L² T⁻²] is the dimension of work and energy. Force is [M L T⁻²], momentum [M L T⁻¹] and pressure [M L⁻¹ T⁻²].

courses.title: Ch 2 · Motion in a Straight Line
courses.summary: Position, displacement, velocity and acceleration in one dimension; motion graphs; derivations of the kinematic equations; free fall and relative velocity.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish distance from displacement and speed from velocity
Learners can read and draw x–t and v–t graphs and use slopes and areas
Learners can derive and apply the three equations of uniformly accelerated motion
Learners can solve free-fall and relative-velocity problems

scenes.text: An auto goes 360 m east to drop a parcel, then comes back 120 m to pick up Meena.
Meena notices the meter charged for 480 m, but she is only 240 m from the start. Distance and displacement are different!

steps.title: Key definitions
steps.body:
- **Position** x: location relative to a chosen origin on a line, with sign showing direction.
- **Displacement** Δx = x₂ − x₁ (vector; can be negative or zero).
- **Path length (distance)**: total length travelled (scalar, never negative).
- **Average velocity** = Δx / Δt (vector).
- **Average speed** = path length / time (scalar). Average speed ≥ |average velocity|.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A car goes 360 m east in 18 s, then 120 m west in 6 s.
- Displacement = 360 − 120 = 240 m east; distance = 480 m; time = 24 s
- Average velocity = 240/24 = **10 m/s east**; average speed = 480/24 = **20 m/s**

**Example 2:** A runner completes one full lap of a 400 m track in 50 s.
- Displacement = 0 → average velocity = 0
- Average speed = 400/50 = **8 m/s**

steps.title: Sign convention
steps.body: Choose one direction as positive and stick to it for position, velocity and acceleration. A negative velocity just means motion in the negative direction — not 'slowing down'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Averaging speeds directly: going 30 km/h one way and 60 km/h back over the same distance gives average speed 40 km/h, not 45 (use total distance / total time).
- Treating distance and displacement as equal when the motion reverses.

activity.prompt: A cyclist rides 6 km at 12 km/h and returns the same 6 km at 6 km/h. What is the average speed for the round trip?

quiz.q: A body moves on a circle of radius r and completes half a revolution. Displacement is
quiz.why: After half a revolution, the body is at the opposite end of a diameter, so the displacement is the straight-line distance 2r. The path length would be πr.

quiz.q: Average speed is always
options: greater than or equal to |average velocity|
quiz.why: Average speed = total path length/time and |average velocity| = |displacement|/time. The path length is never less than the displacement, so average speed ≥ |average velocity|.

quiz.q: Displacement can be
quiz.why: Displacement is a vector along the line, so it can be positive, negative (opposite direction) or zero (returning to the start).

quiz.q: A man walks 4 m east then 3 m west in 7 s. Average velocity is
quiz.why: The net displacement is 4 − 3 = 1 m east. Average velocity = displacement/time = 1/7 m/s east, not distance/time.

quiz.q: Equal distances at speeds v₁ and v₂: average speed =
quiz.why: For equal distances d at speeds v₁ and v₂, total time = d/v₁ + d/v₂, so average speed = 2d/(d/v₁ + d/v₂) = 2v₁v₂/(v₁ + v₂), the harmonic mean, not the simple average.

lessons.title: Instantaneous velocity, acceleration and motion graphs

scenes.text: A bike-taxi app plots position against time. The curve gets steeper.
Steeper slope means higher velocity. Sami learns to read speed straight off a graph.

steps.title: Instantaneous quantities
steps.body:
- **Instantaneous velocity** v = dx/dt = slope of the x–t graph at that instant.
- **Average acceleration** = Δv/Δt; **instantaneous acceleration** a = dv/dt = d²x/dt² = slope of the v–t graph.
- **Area under the v–t graph** between two times = displacement.
- Area under the a–t graph = change in velocity.

If v and a have the same sign the object speeds up; opposite signs → it slows down.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** x = 8.5 + 2.5t² (x in m, t in s). Find v and a at t = 2 s.
- v = dx/dt = 5t → v(2) = **10 m/s**
- a = dv/dt = **5 m/s²** (constant)

**Example 2:** v–t graph: velocity rises uniformly from 0 to 20 m/s in 4 s, stays 20 m/s for 6 s, then falls to 0 in 5 s. Total displacement?
- Triangle ½ × 4 × 20 = 40 m; rectangle 6 × 20 = 120 m; triangle ½ × 5 × 20 = 50 m
- Total = **210 m**

steps.title: Graph shapes
steps.body:
- Uniform velocity: straight sloping x–t line; horizontal v–t line.
- Uniform acceleration: parabola on x–t; straight sloping v–t line.
- At rest: horizontal x–t line.
- An x–t graph can never be vertical (infinite speed) or double-valued in time.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading displacement from the HEIGHT of a v–t graph instead of the AREA.
- Assuming zero velocity means zero acceleration — at the top of a vertical throw v = 0 but a = g.
- Counting area below the time axis as positive displacement (it is negative).

statements.s: The slope of an x–t graph gives acceleration.
statements.why: It gives velocity; the slope of v–t gives acceleration.

statements.s: Area under a v–t graph gives displacement.
A body can have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration.
statements.why: Top point of a vertical throw.

statements.s: An x–t graph can be a vertical line.
If v and a are opposite in sign, the object slows down.
statements.why: Acceleration reduces the magnitude of velocity.

quiz.q: For x = 3t³ m, acceleration at t = 1 s is
quiz.why: Differentiate x = 3t³: v = 9t², a = 18t. At t = 1 s, a = 18 m/s².

quiz.q: A straight v–t line with positive slope indicates
quiz.why: The slope of a v–t graph is acceleration. A straight line has a constant slope, so the acceleration is uniform (and positive here).

quiz.q: Area under an acceleration–time graph is
quiz.why: The area under an acceleration–time graph is ∫a dt, which equals the change in velocity. The area under a v–t graph gives displacement.

quiz.q: A ball thrown up: at the top,
quiz.why: At the highest point the velocity is momentarily zero, but gravity still acts, so the acceleration is g downward.

quiz.q: x–t graph of uniformly accelerated motion from rest is a
quiz.why: Starting from rest with constant acceleration x = ½at², which is quadratic in t, so the x–t graph is a parabola.

scenes.text: A car at 126 km/h sees a stalled truck. The driver brakes hard and stops in 200 m.
Using v² = u² + 2as, the class finds the deceleration and stopping time — and why speed limits matter.

steps.title: The three equations (constant a)
steps.body:
- v = u + at
- s = ut + ½at²
- v² = u² + 2as

Also: displacement in the nth second sₙ = u + a(2n − 1)/2, and s = (u + v)t/2.

**Graphical derivation:** on a v–t straight line from u to v over time t, slope = a gives v = u + at; area (rectangle ut + triangle ½(v − u)t) gives s = ut + ½at². Eliminating t gives v² = u² + 2as.

**Calculus derivation:** a = dv/dt → ∫dv = ∫a dt → v = u + at; v = dx/dt → x = ut + ½at²; a = v dv/dx → v² − u² = 2as.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** u = 126 km/h = 35 m/s, stops in 200 m.
- 0 = 35² + 2a(200) → a = −1225/400 = **−3.06 m/s²**
- t = (0 − 35)/(−3.06) ≈ **11.4 s**

**Example 2:** A ball is thrown up at 20 m/s from the top of a 25 m building (g = 10 m/s²). When does it hit the ground?
- Take up as positive, origin at roof: −25 = 20t − 5t²
- t² − 4t − 5 = 0 → (t − 5)(t + 1) = 0 → **t = 5 s**
- Max height above roof = u²/2g = 400/20 = 20 m

steps.title: Free fall
steps.body:
Neglecting air resistance, all bodies near Earth fall with a = g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downward. From rest: v = gt, h = ½gt², v² = 2gh.

**Galileo's law of odd numbers:** distances fallen in successive equal intervals from rest are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 …

**Stopping distance** ∝ u²: doubling speed makes braking distance four times.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using kinematic equations when acceleration is NOT constant.
- Mixing sign conventions (taking g positive while upward velocity is also positive).
- Forgetting to convert km/h to m/s.
- Rejecting the negative root without thinking — check which root is physical.

activity.prompt: A stone is dropped from rest from a height of 80 m (g = 10 m/s²). How many seconds does it take to reach the ground?

quiz.q: A body starts from rest with a = 2 m/s². Distance in the 5th second is
quiz.why: Distance in the nth second = u + a(2n − 1)/2. With u = 0, a = 2 and n = 5, that is 2 × 9/2 = 9 m. (25 m is the distance in 5 seconds.)

quiz.q: If initial speed doubles, braking distance (same deceleration) becomes
quiz.why: With v = 0, stopping distance s = u²/(2a). Doubling u makes u² four times larger, so the distance becomes four times.

quiz.q: Ratio of distances fallen in 1st, 2nd and 3rd seconds of free fall is
quiz.why: From rest, distances in successive seconds are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 (odd numbers), which is Galileo's law for free fall.

quiz.q: A ball thrown up at 30 m/s (g = 10) reaches maximum height
quiz.why: Maximum height H = u²/2g = 900/20 = 45 m.

quiz.q: Kinematic equations apply when
quiz.why: The kinematic equations of motion are derived assuming constant acceleration, so they apply only in that case.

scenes.text: A bus at 60 km/h is overtaken by a car at 80 km/h. To the bus passengers the car seems to crawl past.
On a parallel track, a train coming the other way at 40 km/h seems to rush past at 100 km/h.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
Velocity of A relative to B: **v_AB = v_A − v_B**. Similarly v_BA = v_B − v_A = −v_AB.

Relative position x_BA = x_B − x_A changes at rate v_BA. If v_A = v_B, the separation stays constant (x–t lines parallel). Same direction: relative speed = difference; opposite directions: relative speed = sum.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Car 80 km/h and bus 60 km/h, same direction.
- v_car,bus = 80 − 60 = **20 km/h** forward

**Example 2:** Two trains 100 m and 150 m long move in opposite directions at 15 m/s and 10 m/s. Time to cross each other?
- Relative speed = 25 m/s; distance = 100 + 150 = 250 m
- t = 250/25 = **10 s**

**Example 3:** Two cars 1 km apart move toward each other at 54 km/h (15 m/s) and 36 km/h (10 m/s). They meet after 1000/25 = **40 s**.

steps.title: Trick
steps.body: Freeze one body: give both bodies a velocity equal and opposite to the one you freeze. Then only one body moves, with the relative velocity, and the problem becomes simple.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Getting the order wrong: v_AB is A as seen from B (A minus B).
- Forgetting to add both train lengths when trains cross.
- Mixing km/h and m/s.

activity.prompt: Complete the statement
activity.text: Two bodies moving in opposite directions at 20 m/s and 30 m/s have relative speed ___ m/s; in the same direction it is ___ m/s.

quiz.q: A at +10 m/s, B at −5 m/s. v_AB =
quiz.why: The relative velocity of A with respect to B is v_A − v_B = 10 − (−5) = 15 m/s.

quiz.q: Two cars with equal velocity: x–t graphs are
quiz.why: Equal velocity means equal slope on x–t graphs, so the lines are parallel and the separation stays constant.

quiz.q: A 200 m train at 20 m/s crosses a 300 m bridge in
quiz.why: The train must cover its own length plus the bridge: 200 + 300 = 500 m. At 20 m/s the time is 500/20 = 25 s.

quiz.q: v_BA equals
quiz.why: v_BA = v_B − v_A = −(v_A − v_B) = −v_AB. Swapping the observer reverses the sign.

quiz.q: Two trains 120 m each at 36 km/h and 54 km/h in the same direction. Time for the faster to pass the slower:
quiz.why: 36 km/h = 10 m/s and 54 km/h = 15 m/s, so the relative speed is 5 m/s. To pass, the faster train must gain 120 + 120 = 240 m, so t = 240/5 = 48 s.

questions.q: The slope of a velocity–time graph gives
questions.why: The slope of a velocity–time graph is dv/dt, which is the acceleration.

questions.q: Odometer measures
questions.why: An odometer records the total path length travelled, i.e. distance, and not displacement.

questions.q: A body moving with uniform velocity has acceleration
questions.why: Uniform velocity means the velocity does not change with time, so the acceleration is zero.

questions.q: x = 2t² − 4t. Velocity is zero at
questions.why: v = dx/dt = 4t − 4. Setting v = 0 gives t = 1 s.

questions.q: A car accelerates from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 s. Distance covered:
questions.why: With uniform acceleration, s = (u + v)t/2 = (10 + 30)/2 × 5 = 20 × 5 = 100 m.

questions.q: Assertion: A body can have constant speed but varying velocity. Reason: Velocity includes direction.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Velocity is a vector with direction, so even at constant speed the velocity changes if the direction changes, as in motion on a circle.

questions.q: A ball dropped from 45 m (g = 10) hits the ground with speed
questions.why: Using v² = 2gh = 2 × 10 × 45 = 900, so v = 30 m/s.

questions.q: Distance travelled in the 3rd second by a body starting from rest with a = 4 m/s²:
questions.why: Distance in the nth second = a(2n − 1)/2 for a start from rest. With a = 4 and n = 3: 4 × 5/2 = 10 m.

questions.q: Case: A cricket ball is thrown up with 20 m/s and caught at the same height (g = 10). Total time in air?
questions.why: The ball returns to the same height after T = 2u/g = 2 × 20/10 = 4 s (2 s up and 2 s down).

questions.q: A train starting from rest accelerates at 1 m/s² for 10 s, moves uniformly for 30 s, then decelerates to rest in 5 s. Total distance:
questions.why: After 10 s the speed is 10 m/s. Distances: ½ × 10 × 10 = 50 m, then 10 × 30 = 300 m, then ½ × 10 × 5 = 25 m. Total = 375 m.

questions.q: A stone is thrown up from a 40 m tower at 10 m/s (g = 10). Time to reach the ground:
questions.why: Taking up as positive, displacement = −40 m: −40 = 10t − 5t², so t² − 2t − 8 = 0 and (t − 4)(t + 2) = 0. The valid time is t = 4 s.

questions.q: Two balls are dropped from heights h and 4h. Ratio of their times of fall:
questions.why: From h = ½gt², time of fall t ∝ √h. For heights h and 4h the ratio of times is √1 : √4 = 1 : 2.

questions.q: A body covers 20 m in the 2nd second and 40 m in the 4th second (uniform a). Its acceleration is
questions.why: The distance in the nth second is u + a(2n − 1)/2. So s₄ − s₂ = a(7 − 3)/2 = 2a. Here 40 − 20 = 20 = 2a, so a = 10 m/s².

questions.q: Velocity v of a particle varies with position as v = α√x. Its acceleration is
questions.why: a = v dv/dx. With v = α√x, dv/dx = α/(2√x), so a = α√x × α/(2√x) = α²/2, a constant.

questions.q: Car A (25 m/s) is 100 m behind car B (15 m/s), same lane and direction. Time for A to catch B:
questions.why: A gains on B at the relative speed 25 − 15 = 10 m/s. To close a gap of 100 m takes 100/10 = 10 s.

questions.q: An x–t graph is a straight line parallel to the time axis. The body is
questions.why: A horizontal line on an x–t graph means the position does not change with time, so the body is at rest.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Motion in a Plane
courses.summary: Vectors and their algebra, motion in two dimensions with constant acceleration, projectile motion with full derivations, and uniform circular motion.
outcomes: Learners can add, subtract and resolve vectors graphically and analytically
Learners can describe 2D motion with position, velocity and acceleration vectors
Learners can derive time of flight, maximum height, range and trajectory of a projectile
Learners can compute centripetal acceleration in uniform circular motion

scenes.text: Two friends pull a cart with ropes at an angle. Each pulls with 10 N.
The cart does not feel 20 N — it feels about 17 N. Direction matters, so forces add as vectors.

steps.title: Vectors and their properties
steps.body:
- **Scalar**: magnitude only (mass, time, energy). **Vector**: magnitude and direction, obeys triangle/parallelogram law (displacement, force, velocity).
- Equal vectors: same magnitude and direction. Negative vector −A: same magnitude, opposite direction.
- Multiplying by a scalar λ scales magnitude by |λ| (and reverses direction if λ < 0).
- Addition is commutative and associative. A − B = A + (−B).
- **Null vector** 0: zero magnitude, e.g. A + (−A).

steps.title: Analytical addition and resolution
steps.body:
Resultant of A and B with angle θ between them:
- R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ)
- tan α = B sin θ / (A + B cos θ), α measured from A

**Resolution:** A = Aₓ î + A_y ĵ with Aₓ = A cos θ, A_y = A sin θ; |A| = √(Aₓ² + A_y²), tan θ = A_y/Aₓ.

Add components: R = (Aₓ + Bₓ) î + (A_y + B_y) ĵ. Unit vectors î, ĵ, k̂ have magnitude 1 along x, y, z.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** 3 N and 4 N at 90°.
- R = √(9 + 16) = **5 N**; tan α = 4/3 → α ≈ 53° from the 3 N force

**Example 2:** Two 10 N forces at 60°.
- R = √(100 + 100 + 200 × 0.5) = √300 = **17.3 N**, along the bisector (30° from each)

**Example 3:** A = 3î + 4ĵ, B = î − 2ĵ. Find A + B and |A − B|.
- A + B = 4î + 2ĵ; A − B = 2î + 6ĵ → |A − B| = √40 ≈ **6.32**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding magnitudes directly when vectors are not parallel.
- Using the angle between head and tail instead of between the vectors drawn tail to tail.
- Thinking the resultant must exceed each vector — range is |A − B| ≤ R ≤ A + B.
- Treating current as a vector (it has direction but does not add by vector law).

bands.text: 120°: R = 10 N — equal to each force.

quiz.q: Resultant of two equal forces F at 120° is
quiz.why: For two equal forces F at angle θ, R = √(F² + F² + 2F² cos θ). With θ = 120°, cos θ = −1/2, so R = √(2F² − F²) = F.

quiz.q: Which is a vector?
quiz.why: Impulse is force × time and has a direction (that of the change in momentum), so it is a vector. Work, current and temperature are scalars.
The magnitude is √(3² + (−4)²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5.

quiz.q: Two forces 5 N and 8 N can NOT have a resultant of
quiz.why: The resultant of 5 N and 8 N lies between their difference (3 N) and their sum (13 N). So 2 N is impossible.

quiz.q: Component of a 20 N force at 30° to the x-axis along x:
quiz.why: The component along x is F cos θ = 20 cos 30° = 20 × 0.866 ≈ 17.3 N. The component along y would be 10 N.

lessons.title: Motion in a plane and relative velocity in 2D

scenes.text: Rain falls straight down, but as Neha cycles fast, the rain seems to hit her face.
She tilts her umbrella forward — along the relative velocity of rain with respect to her.

steps.title: Position, velocity and acceleration vectors
steps.body:
- Position r = x î + y ĵ; velocity v = dr/dt = vₓ î + v_y ĵ (always tangent to the path).
- Acceleration a = dv/dt.
- With constant a: **v = u + at** and **r = r₀ + ut + ½at²** — these split into independent x and y equations. This is the key idea: motion in a plane = two independent 1D motions.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** r = 3t î + 2t² ĵ (m). Find v and a at t = 1 s.
- v = 3 î + 4t ĵ → at t = 1: 3î + 4ĵ, |v| = **5 m/s**
- a = 4 ĵ m/s² (constant, along y)

**Example 2:** Rain falls vertically at 35 m/s; wind blows east at 12 m/s.
- Resultant speed = √(35² + 12²) = √1369 = **37 m/s**
- Angle with vertical: tan θ = 12/35 → θ ≈ **19°** towards east — hold umbrella tilted that way.

**Example 3:** A boat at 4 km/h (relative to water) heads straight across a river flowing at 3 km/h. Resultant speed 5 km/h; it drifts downstream.

steps.title: River-boat ideas
steps.body:
- To cross in **minimum time**, head perpendicular to the flow: t = width / v_boat.
- To cross along the **shortest path** (straight across), head upstream at angle θ with sin θ = v_river / v_boat (possible only if v_boat > v_river).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking acceleration must be along the velocity — in a projectile it is downward while v is slanted.
- Subtracting speeds instead of vectors in 2D relative motion.
- Mixing up 'angle with vertical' and 'angle with horizontal'.

activity.prompt: A swimmer swims at 5 m/s relative to water, straight across a river 100 m wide that flows at 3 m/s. How long (in s) does she take to cross?

quiz.q: r = 2t² î + 3t ĵ. Acceleration is
quiz.why: Differentiate r = 2t² î + 3t ĵ once: v = 4t î + 3 ĵ. Again: a = 4 î (the ĵ term is constant, so it vanishes).

quiz.q: Velocity of a particle is always
quiz.why: Velocity v = dr/dt is always tangent to the particle's path. Acceleration need not be along it.

quiz.q: A man walks at 4 km/h; rain falls vertically at 3 km/h. Relative speed of rain to man:
quiz.why: Rain relative to the man = rain velocity − man velocity. The speed is √(4² + 3²) = √25 = 5 km/h.

quiz.q: To cross a river in minimum time, a boat should head
quiz.why: The component of the boat's velocity across the river decides the crossing time, and it is largest when the boat heads perpendicular to the flow, so the time is least.

quiz.q: Motion in a plane with constant acceleration can be treated as
quiz.why: With constant acceleration, the x and y components of motion are independent, so each can be treated as a separate one-dimensional motion.

sources: NCERT Physics Class 11 (topic: motion in a plane)

scenes.text: A fielder throws the ball at 20 m/s. At what angle should he throw to reach the keeper farthest away?
Physics says 45° for maximum range on level ground — and 30° and 60° give the same range!

steps.title: Derivations
steps.body:
Launch speed u at angle θ; take aₓ = 0, a_y = −g.
- x = (u cos θ) t; y = (u sin θ) t − ½gt²
- **Trajectory:** eliminate t → y = x tan θ − g x² / (2u² cos² θ), a parabola.
- **Time of flight:** y = 0 → T = 2u sin θ / g
- **Maximum height:** v_y = 0 → H = u² sin² θ / (2g)
- **Horizontal range:** R = (u cos θ)T = u² sin 2θ / g; maximum R = u²/g at θ = 45°.
- θ and (90° − θ) give the same range.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°, g = 10 m/s².
- T = 2 × 20 × 0.5/10 = **2 s**
- H = 400 × 0.25/20 = **5 m**
- R = 400 × sin 60°/10 = 40 × 0.866 = **34.6 m**

**Example 2:** A ball is thrown horizontally at 10 m/s from a cliff 45 m high (g = 10).
- Time: 45 = ½ × 10 × t² → t = **3 s**
- Horizontal distance = 10 × 3 = **30 m**
- Speed on impact = √(10² + 30²) ≈ 31.6 m/s

steps.title: Handy relations
steps.body:
- At the top, speed = u cos θ (only horizontal) and acceleration = g downward.
- tan θ = 4H/R.
- When R is maximum (θ = 45°), H = R/4.
- Air resistance reduces range and height and makes the path non-symmetric.

steps.title: Common mistakes
