questions.why: The extension ΔL = FL/(AY) ∝ L/r². With L doubled and r doubled, the ratio is 2/4 = 1/2, so the extension is ΔL/2.

questions.q: Case: A 1 m long steel rod (A = 1 cm², Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa) is compressed by a 20 kN force. Change in length:
questions.why: ΔL = FL/(AY) = (2 × 10⁴ × 1)/(10⁻⁴ × 2 × 10¹¹) = 10⁻³ m = 1 mm. 1 cm² must be converted to 10⁻⁴ m².

questions.q: Pressure needed to compress water (B = 2.2 × 10⁹ Pa) by 0.1%:
Energy stored in a wire with stress 2 × 10⁸ Pa and Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa per unit volume:
questions.why: Energy density u = σ²/(2Y) = (2 × 10⁸)²/(2 × 2 × 10¹¹) = 4 × 10¹⁶/(4 × 10¹¹) = 10⁵ J/m³.

questions.q: A beam's depth is doubled keeping other things same. Sag at the centre becomes
questions.why: A beam's sag varies as 1/d³. If the depth doubles, sag becomes 1/2³ = 1/8.

questions.q: Two wires A and B of the same material: A has double the length and double the diameter of B. Same load. Ratio of extensions A:B:
questions.why: Extension ∝ L/d². A has double the length and double the diameter, so the ratio is 2/4 = 1/2, that is A : B = 1 : 2.

questions.q: A steel wire of 2 mm² cross-section and yield strength 2.5 × 10⁸ Pa. Maximum load it can bear without permanent set:
questions.why: Maximum load = yield strength × area = 2.5 × 10⁸ × 2 × 10⁻⁶ m² = 500 N. Convert mm² to m² (1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m²).

questions.q: A rubber cord (Y = 5 × 10⁸ Pa, A = 1 mm²) of length 10 cm is stretched to 12 cm. Elastic energy stored (assume Hooke's law holds):
questions.why: Strain 0.2; u = ½Yε² = ½ × 5 × 10⁸ × 0.04 = 10⁷ J/m³; volume = 10⁻⁶ × 0.1 = 10⁻⁷ m³ → U = 1 J.

questions.q: Shear modulus is also called
questions.why: The shear modulus is also called the modulus of rigidity; it measures resistance to change of shape.

questions.q: A load W on a wire produces extension e. Work done by the load as it is applied gradually equals
questions.why: When the load increases gradually from 0 to W, the average force is W/2, so the work done is (W/2) × e = We/2.

school-c11-physics-c.title: Class 11 Physics · Part C (Ch 9–11)
school-c11-physics-c.description: Class 11 Physics chapter by chapter: Mechanical Properties of Fluids, Thermal Properties of Matter and Thermodynamics — derivations, solved numericals and JEE/NEET bridge practice.

courses.title: Ch 9 · Mechanical Properties of Fluids
courses.summary: Pressure and Pascal's law, hydraulic machines, streamline flow and the equation of continuity, Bernoulli's principle with applications, viscosity and Stokes' law, Reynolds number, surface tension and capillarity.
outcomes: Learners can compute pressure at depth and apply Pascal's law
Learners can use the continuity equation and Bernoulli's principle
Learners can derive terminal velocity from Stokes' law
Learners can compute excess pressure in drops and bubbles and capillary rise

lessons.title: Pressure, Pascal's law and hydraulic machines

scenes.text: At a service station, a mechanic lifts a whole car by pressing a small lever.
Inside, oil transmits pressure equally to a big piston. Small force × large area ratio = huge lifting force.

steps.title: Pressure in a fluid
steps.body:
- Pressure P = F/A (Pa = N/m²); 1 atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa.
- At depth h in a liquid of density ρ: **P = Pₐ + ρgh**. Gauge pressure = P − Pₐ = ρgh.
- Pressure is the same at all points at the same depth in a connected static fluid, regardless of container shape (**hydrostatic paradox**).
- Mercury barometer: Pₐ = ρgh, h ≈ 76 cm of Hg at sea level.

steps.title: Pascal's law
steps.body:
Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and the container walls.

**Hydraulic lift:** F₂ = F₁ × (A₂/A₁). Work in = work out (ideal): the small piston moves farther. Used in hydraulic brakes, jacks, presses.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Pressure 10 m below a lake surface (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8).
- P = 1.01 × 10⁵ + 1000 × 9.8 × 10 = **1.99 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 2 atm**

**Example 2:** Hydraulic lift: small piston 0.01 m², large piston 0.5 m², effort 100 N.
- F₂ = 100 × 50 = **5000 N**

**Example 3:** A 50 kg girl stands on one heel of area 1 cm². P = 490/10⁻⁴ = **4.9 × 10⁶ Pa** — why stiletto heels dent floors.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to add atmospheric pressure when absolute pressure is asked.
- Thinking pressure depends on container shape.
- Expecting a hydraulic lift to multiply energy — it multiplies force only.

activity.prompt: Gauge pressure at 5 m depth in water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s²) in kPa?

quiz.q: Pressure at the same depth in a static liquid is
quiz.why: In a static liquid the pressure depends only on depth (p = ρgh), so points at the same depth have the same pressure, whatever the shape of the vessel.

quiz.q: 1 atm is about
quiz.why: One standard atmosphere is about 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa (760 mm of mercury).

quiz.q: Hydraulic brakes work on
quiz.why: Hydraulic brakes use Pascal's law: pressure applied to the brake fluid is transmitted equally through it to all the wheel cylinders.

quiz.q: Area ratio of pistons is 1:20. Effort 50 N gives load
quiz.why: In a hydraulic machine, pressure is the same, so the force is in the ratio of areas. The load is 50 N × 20 = 1000 N. (The output piston is larger.)

quiz.q: Gauge pressure equals
quiz.why: Gauge pressure is the pressure above the atmospheric pressure: absolute pressure − atmospheric pressure.

sources: NCERT Physics Class 11 (topic: pressure in fluids)

lessons.title: Streamline flow, continuity and Bernoulli's principle

scenes.text: Kiran presses his thumb over the hose mouth and the water shoots much farther.
The same physics — continuity and Bernoulli — explains why aeroplane wings get lift.

steps.title: Flow and continuity
steps.body:
- **Streamline (steady) flow:** velocity at each point stays constant in time; streamlines never cross.
- **Turbulent flow:** irregular, at high speeds.
- **Equation of continuity** (incompressible fluid): **A₁v₁ = A₂v₂** — mass conservation. Narrower tube → faster flow.

steps.title: Bernoulli's principle
steps.body:
Along a streamline of steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow:
**P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant.**

**Derivation idea:** work done by pressure forces (P₁ − P₂)ΔV equals the gain in kinetic and potential energy of the fluid element ½ρΔV(v₂² − v₁²) + ρΔVg(h₂ − h₁).

Applications:
- **Torricelli's law:** speed of efflux from a hole at depth h: v = √(2gh).
- **Venturimeter:** measures flow speed from a pressure difference.
- **Dynamic lift** on wings and spinning balls (Magnus effect); blowing between two sheets brings them together; roofs blown off in storms.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Water flows at 2 m/s in a pipe; the pipe narrows to half the radius.
- Area becomes 1/4 → v = **8 m/s**

**Example 2:** Hole 5 m below the water surface in a tank (g = 10).
- v = √(2 × 10 × 5) = **10 m/s**

**Example 3:** Air speeds over and under a wing are 70 m/s and 63 m/s (ρ_air = 1.3 kg/m³). Pressure difference = ½ × 1.3 × (4900 − 3969) ≈ **605 Pa** upward.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying Bernoulli to viscous or turbulent flow without caution.
- Thinking faster fluid has higher pressure — it is the opposite along a streamline.
- Forgetting to square radius ratios in continuity problems.

statements.s: In a narrower section of a pipe, water flows faster.
Where speed is higher along a streamline, pressure is higher.
Speed of efflux from a hole depends on the depth below the free surface.
Streamlines can cross each other.
statements.why: That would give two velocities at one point.

quiz.q: Equation of continuity expresses conservation of
quiz.why: The equation of continuity (Av = constant) expresses conservation of mass for the flow of an incompressible fluid.

quiz.q: Bernoulli's equation is a statement of conservation of
quiz.why: Bernoulli's equation is the work–energy principle applied to fluid flow, so it expresses conservation of energy.

quiz.q: Speed of efflux from a hole 20 m below the surface (g = 10):
Lift on an aeroplane wing is due to
quiz.why: The wing shape makes air move faster over the top, so by Bernoulli's principle the pressure above is lower than below. This pressure difference gives lift.

quiz.q: Pipe diameter halves. Speed becomes
quiz.why: Area ∝ d². Halving the diameter makes the area 1/4, so by Av = constant the speed becomes 4 times.

lessons.title: Viscosity, Stokes' law and Reynolds number

scenes.text: Honey crawls out of the jar; water pours instantly.
Raindrops stop speeding up after a while — air's viscous drag balances gravity at terminal velocity.

steps.title: Viscosity
steps.body:
Internal friction between fluid layers in relative motion. **F = −ηA(dv/dx)**; η = coefficient of viscosity (SI: Pa s = N s m⁻²; CGS: poise, 1 poise = 0.1 Pa s).
- For liquids η decreases as temperature rises; for gases it increases.

steps.title: Stokes' law and terminal velocity
steps.body:
Drag on a sphere of radius r moving slowly at v: **F = 6πηrv**.

Terminal velocity (weight = buoyancy + drag):
**v_t = 2r²(ρ − σ)g / (9η)** where ρ = density of sphere, σ = density of fluid. v_t ∝ r².

**Reynolds number** Re = ρvd/η (dimensionless): Re < about 1000 → streamline; Re > about 2000 → turbulent.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A raindrop of radius 0.3 mm in air (η = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ Pa s), ignoring air density.
- v_t = 2 × (3 × 10⁻⁴)² × 1000 × 9.8/(9 × 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) ≈ **10.9 m/s** (real drops are slower because the flow becomes turbulent)

**Example 2:** Two drops each with terminal speed v merge into one. New radius = 2^(1/3) r → v' = 2^(2/3) v ≈ **1.59 v**.

**Example 3:** Water (η = 10⁻³ Pa s) flows at 0.1 m/s in a 1 cm pipe. Re = 1000 × 0.1 × 0.01/10⁻³ = **1000** — near the laminar limit.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using diameter instead of radius in Stokes' formula.
- Forgetting buoyancy (ρ − σ).
- Thinking gas viscosity falls with temperature like liquids.

activity.prompt: Complete
activity.text: Terminal velocity varies as the ___ of the radius; the SI unit of viscosity is ___.

quiz.q: Stokes' drag force is
quiz.why: Stokes' law gives the viscous drag on a sphere of radius r moving at speed v as F = 6πηrv.

quiz.q: Viscosity of a liquid with rising temperature
quiz.why: The viscosity of a liquid decreases as temperature rises, because the molecular cohesion weakens (for gases it increases).

quiz.q: Terminal velocity is reached when
quiz.why: Terminal velocity is reached when the weight is balanced by drag and buoyancy, so the net force is zero and the body stops accelerating.

quiz.q: Reynolds number is
quiz.why: The Reynolds number is the ratio of inertial to viscous forces, so it has no dimensions.

quiz.q: If radius doubles, terminal velocity becomes
quiz.why: Terminal velocity is proportional to r². Doubling the radius makes it 2² = 4 times as large.

lessons.title: Surface tension, drops, bubbles and capillarity

scenes.text: A water strider walks on the pond surface without sinking.
Back home, Lata watches wax climb up a candle wick. Surface tension and capillarity are at work in both.

steps.title: Surface tension and surface energy
steps.body:
Molecules at a liquid surface have extra energy because they lack neighbours on one side.
- **Surface tension** S = force per unit length along a line on the surface = surface energy per unit area (N/m = J/m²).
- Work to increase area by ΔA: W = SΔA (a soap film has two surfaces → 2SΔA).
- S decreases as temperature rises; detergents lower S.
- **Angle of contact** θ: acute for water–glass (wets), obtuse for mercury–glass (does not wet).

steps.title: Excess pressure and capillary rise
steps.body:
- Liquid drop or air bubble inside a liquid: **ΔP = 2S/r**
- Soap bubble in air (two surfaces): **ΔP = 4S/r**
- **Capillary rise:** h = 2S cos θ/(ρgr). Water rises in glass; mercury is depressed (cos θ < 0). Narrower tube → higher rise.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Water (S = 0.073 N/m) in a glass capillary of radius 0.05 cm, θ ≈ 0.
- h = 2 × 0.073/(1000 × 9.8 × 5 × 10⁻⁴) ≈ **2.98 cm**

**Example 2:** Excess pressure inside a water drop of radius 1 mm: 2 × 0.073/10⁻³ = **146 Pa**.

**Example 3:** Work to blow a soap bubble (S = 0.03 N/m) of radius 1 cm: W = S × 2 × 4πr² = 0.03 × 8π × 10⁻⁴ ≈ **7.5 × 10⁻⁵ J**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the two surfaces of a soap bubble (4S/r, not 2S/r).
- Using diameter for r in capillary formulas.
- Thinking surface tension is a force per area — it is per length.

activity.prompt: Which effect is mainly responsible?

items.text: Water rising in a thin glass tube
Roof blown off in a cyclone
Terminal velocity of a falling drop

quiz.q: SI unit of surface tension
quiz.why: Surface tension is force per unit length, so its SI unit is N/m (equivalently J/m²).

quiz.q: Excess pressure inside a soap bubble
quiz.why: A soap bubble has two surfaces (inside and outside), so the excess pressure is 2 × 2S/r = 4S/r. A drop with one surface has 2S/r.

quiz.q: Mercury in a glass capillary
quiz.why: Mercury does not wet glass (obtuse angle of contact), so it is depressed in a glass capillary instead of rising.

quiz.q: Capillary rise is greater in
quiz.why: Capillary rise is h = 2S cos θ/(ρgr), so it is inversely proportional to the radius. Narrower tubes give a larger rise.

quiz.q: Adding detergent to water
quiz.why: Detergents are surfactants that lower the surface tension of water, which helps it wet and clean surfaces.

questions.q: Unit of viscosity
questions.why: From F = ηA dv/dx, η = F/(A dv/dx), whose unit is N s m⁻² = Pa s.

questions.q: Pascal's law is used in
questions.why: A hydraulic lift works on Pascal's law, that pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted equally.

questions.q: Raindrops are spherical because of
questions.why: Surface tension tries to minimise the surface area of a liquid drop, and a sphere has the least surface for a given volume, so raindrops are spherical.

questions.q: Pressure 20 m under water (gauge, g = 10)
questions.why: Gauge pressure = ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 20 = 2 × 10⁵ Pa.

questions.q: Assertion: A spinning ball curves in flight. Reason: Pressure differs on its two sides due to different air speeds.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. A spinning ball drags air around it, so air moves faster on one side. By Bernoulli's principle that side has lower pressure, so the ball curves (the Magnus effect).

questions.q: Water flows at 3 m/s through a 4 cm² section. Speed in a 1 cm² section:
questions.why: By the equation of continuity A₁v₁ = A₂v₂: 4 × 3 = 1 × v₂, so v₂ = 12 m/s. The speed rises as the section narrows.

questions.q: Excess pressure in an air bubble of radius 0.1 mm in water (S = 0.07 N/m):
questions.why: An air bubble in water has one surface, so the excess pressure is 2S/r = 2 × 0.07/(10⁻⁴) = 1400 Pa. (0.1 mm = 10⁻⁴ m.)

questions.q: Case: A tank 1.8 m deep has a small hole at its bottom (g = 10). Water leaves at
questions.why: Using Torricelli's law, v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 1.8) = √36 = 6 m/s.

questions.q: Two capillaries of radii r and 2r in water. Ratio of rises
questions.why: Capillary rise h ∝ 1/r. For radii r and 2r, the rises are in the ratio 2 : 1 (the narrower tube has the larger rise).

questions.q: Eight identical drops each with terminal speed v merge. New terminal speed:
questions.why: Volume is conserved, so 8 drops make one drop of radius 2r. Terminal velocity ∝ r², so it becomes 4v.

questions.q: Work done to blow a soap bubble of radius r (surface tension S):
questions.why: A soap bubble has two surfaces, each of area 4πr². The work done is S × (increase in area) = S × 2 × 4πr² = 8πr²S.

questions.q: Water rises 6 cm in a capillary on Earth. On a planet with g/3 it would rise
questions.why: Capillary rise h = 2S cos θ/(ρgr) is proportional to 1/g. With g/3 the rise becomes 3 × 6 = 18 cm.

questions.q: A hydraulic press has pistons of diameter 2 cm and 20 cm. Force on the small piston to lift 1000 kg (g = 10):
questions.why: Pressure is the same on both pistons, so F₁ = F₂ × (A₁/A₂). Area ratio = (2/20)² = 1/100, so F₁ = 10⁴ N/100 = 100 N (load = 1000 kg × 10 = 10⁴ N).

questions.q: A steel ball (ρ = 7800 kg/m³) of radius 1 mm falls in glycerine (σ = 1260 kg/m³, η = 0.83 Pa s). Terminal velocity (g = 9.8) is about
Air (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³) flows over a wing of area 20 m² at 60 m/s above and 50 m/s below. Lift force:
questions.why: Pressure difference = ½ρ(v₁² − v₂²) = ½ × 1.2 × (3600 − 2500) = 660 Pa. Lift = 660 × 20 = 13,200 N = 13.2 kN.

questions.q: Flow is likely turbulent when Reynolds number is
questions.why: Flow becomes turbulent when the Reynolds number is high, above about 2000 (laminar for low values).

courses.title: Ch 10 · Thermal Properties of Matter
courses.summary: Temperature scales, thermal expansion and the anomalous behaviour of water, specific heat and calorimetry, latent heat, conduction, convection, radiation and Newton's law of cooling.
outcomes: Learners can convert between temperature scales
Learners can calculate linear, area and volume expansion
Learners can solve calorimetry and latent-heat problems
Learners can apply laws of conduction, radiation and Newton's law of cooling

scenes.text: On a summer trip, Nisha spots small gaps between rails.
Steel expands in heat; without gaps the rails would buckle. That is thermal expansion.

steps.title: Temperature scales
steps.body:
- Celsius–Fahrenheit: **t_F = (9/5)t_C + 32**; equal at −40°.
- Kelvin: **T = t_C + 273.15**; absolute zero is 0 K (−273.15 °C).
- Ideal-gas thermometers use PV ∝ T.
- Heat flows because of temperature difference; temperature measures hotness.

steps.title: Thermal expansion
steps.body:
- Linear: ΔL = αLΔT
- Area: ΔA = βAΔT, β = 2α
- Volume: ΔV = γVΔT, γ = 3α (isotropic solids)
- Ideal gas at constant P: γ = 1/T.

**Anomalous expansion of water:** from 0 °C to 4 °C water CONTRACTS; it is densest at 4 °C. Lakes freeze from the top, so water below stays near 4 °C and aquatic life survives.

**Thermal stress** in a clamped rod: stress = YαΔT.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Normal body temperature 37 °C in °F: 9/5 × 37 + 32 = **98.6 °F**.

**Example 2:** A 10 m steel rail (α = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹) heats by 40 K.
- ΔL = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ × 10 × 40 = **4.8 × 10⁻³ m = 4.8 mm**

**Example 3:** A brass rod clamped at both ends (Y = 0.91 × 10¹¹ Pa, α = 2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹) is heated by 50 K. Thermal stress = 0.91 × 10¹¹ × 2 × 10⁻⁵ × 50 ≈ **9.1 × 10⁷ Pa**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing 'degree kelvin' — it is just kelvin (K).
- Using β = α or γ = α.
- Forgetting that a temperature DIFFERENCE of 1 °C equals 1 K but 1.8 °F.

activity.prompt: A temperature reads 212 °F. What is it in kelvin? (use 273)

quiz.q: Celsius and Fahrenheit readings are equal at
quiz.why: Setting C = F: C = 9C/5 + 32 gives −4C/5 = 32, so C = −40. Both scales read −40°.

quiz.q: For an isotropic solid, γ =
quiz.why: For an isotropic solid, the volume expansion coefficient is three times the linear one: γ = 3α (and area coefficient is 2α).

quiz.q: Water is densest at
quiz.why: Water is densest at 4 °C. Between 0 and 4 °C it contracts on heating (anomalous expansion).

quiz.q: Absolute zero in Celsius
quiz.why: Absolute zero (0 K) corresponds to −273.15 °C.

quiz.q: A metal plate with a hole is heated. The hole
quiz.why: When a metal plate with a hole is heated, every dimension, including the hole, expands in the same way as the plate material would, so the hole becomes larger.

story.title: Why the beach is cool at night

scenes.text: At Marina beach the sand burns in the afternoon but the sea stays mild.
Water's large specific heat means it warms and cools slowly — this drives sea breezes.

steps.title: Heat capacity
steps.body:
- Heat Q = mcΔT, c = specific heat capacity (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). Water: c ≈ 4186 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (very high).
- Heat capacity S = mc (J/K).
- Molar specific heat C = Q/(nΔT). For gases Cₚ > C_v because at constant pressure the gas also does work.

**Principle of calorimetry:** in an isolated system, heat lost by hot bodies = heat gained by cold bodies.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** 0.2 kg water at 80 °C is mixed with 0.3 kg water at 20 °C.
- 0.2c(80 − T) = 0.3c(T − 20) → T = (16 + 6)/0.5 = **44 °C**

**Example 2:** A 0.1 kg metal piece at 100 °C is dropped into 0.2 kg water at 20 °C; final temperature 24 °C. Find c_metal (c_water = 4200).
- Heat gained by water = 0.2 × 4200 × 4 = 3360 J
- 0.1 × c × 76 = 3360 → c ≈ **442 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹**

**Example 3:** Energy to heat 2 kg of water from 25 °C to 75 °C = 2 × 4186 × 50 = **4.19 × 10⁵ J**.

steps.title: Why water's high c matters
steps.body: Coolant in car radiators, hot-water bags, moderate coastal climates, and our bodies' stable temperature (we are mostly water) all depend on water's large specific heat.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the container's (calorimeter's) heat.
- Signs: write heat lost = heat gained with positive temperature differences.
- Mixing grams and kilograms with c in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

activity.prompt: How much heat (in kJ) raises 0.5 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C? (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)

quiz.q: Unit of specific heat capacity
quiz.why: Specific heat capacity c = Q/(mΔT), so its unit is J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

quiz.q: For a gas, Cₚ compared to C_v is
quiz.why: For a gas, Cp is greater than Cv, because at constant pressure some heat also does work of expansion (Cp − Cv = R).

quiz.q: Equal masses of water at 10 °C and 50 °C mixed. Final temperature:
quiz.why: With equal masses of the same liquid, the final temperature is the average: (10 + 50)/2 = 30 °C.

quiz.q: Water is used in radiators because it has
quiz.why: Water has a high specific heat, so it can absorb a lot of heat for a small rise in temperature, which makes it a good coolant.

quiz.q: Heat capacity of 2 kg of a material with c = 500 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹:
quiz.why: Heat capacity S = mc = 2 kg × 500 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ = 1000 J/K.

lessons.title: Change of state and latent heat

scenes.text: Mummy's pressure cooker cooks dal faster than an open pan.
Higher pressure raises water's boiling point above 100 °C. And steam burns are worse than boiling-water burns because of latent heat.

steps.title: Change of state
steps.body:
- During melting or boiling, temperature stays constant while heat is absorbed.
- **Latent heat** L: Q = mL. Water: L_f (fusion) ≈ 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg; L_v (vaporisation) ≈ 2.256 × 10⁶ J/kg.
- Boiling point rises with pressure (pressure cooker) and falls at altitude (hills).
- Melting point of ice falls with increased pressure (regelation: a loaded wire passes through an ice block that refreezes above it).
- **Sublimation:** solid → vapour directly (dry ice, camphor, iodine).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Heat to turn 1 kg of ice at 0 °C into steam at 100 °C.
- Melt: 3.34 × 10⁵ J
- Heat water 0 → 100 °C: 1 × 4186 × 100 = 4.186 × 10⁵ J
- Vaporise: 2.256 × 10⁶ J
- Total ≈ **3.01 × 10⁶ J**

**Example 2:** 0.1 kg ice at 0 °C is added to 0.5 kg water at 40 °C. Final temperature?
- Heat to melt ice = 33400 J; water can give 0.5 × 4186 × 40 = 83720 J → all ice melts.
- 0.5 × 4186 × (40 − T) = 33400 + 0.1 × 4186 × T → 83720 − 2093T = 33400 + 418.6T → T ≈ **20 °C**

steps.title: Heating curve
steps.body: A temperature–time graph for heating ice shows: rising slope (ice warms), flat (melting), rising slope (water warms), long flat (boiling — longer because L_v ≫ L_f), rising slope (steam warms).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming all the ice melts — always check available heat first.
- Using ΔT during a phase change (there is none).
- Mixing J/kg and J/g values of latent heat.

activity.prompt: Order the stages when ice at −10 °C is heated to steam at 110 °C
items: Ice warms from −10 °C to 0 °C
Ice melts at 0 °C
Water warms from 0 °C to 100 °C
Water boils at 100 °C
Steam warms from 100 °C to 110 °C

quiz.q: During melting, temperature
quiz.why: During melting, the heat supplied goes into breaking bonds (latent heat), not into raising the temperature, so it stays constant.

quiz.q: Steam at 100 °C causes worse burns than water at 100 °C because
options: steam releases latent heat on condensing
quiz.why: Steam at 100 °C releases the large latent heat of vaporisation (about 2.26 MJ/kg) when it condenses on skin, besides the heat from cooling. Water at 100 °C lacks this extra.

quiz.q: Boiling point at hill stations is
quiz.why: At hill stations the atmospheric pressure is lower, so water boils at a lower temperature.

quiz.q: Heat to melt 2 kg of ice at 0 °C (L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg):
Camphor changing directly to vapour is
quiz.why: Camphor changes directly from solid to vapour without passing through the liquid state, which is sublimation.

lessons.title: Heat transfer and Newton's law of cooling

story.title: The steel tumbler and the clay pot

scenes.text: Hot tea in a steel tumbler burns Ravi's fingers; in a clay kulhad it does not.
Steel conducts heat well, clay poorly. And the tea cools faster when it is hotter — Newton's law of cooling.

steps.title: Conduction, convection, radiation
steps.body:
- **Conduction:** heat flow through matter without bulk motion. Steady state: **H = KA(T_C − T_D)/L**, K = thermal conductivity (W m⁻¹ K⁻¹). Metals high (copper ≈ 385), air and wood low.
- **Convection:** transfer by bulk fluid motion (natural or forced): sea breeze, trade winds, room heaters.
- **Radiation:** by electromagnetic waves, needs no medium. **Stefan–Boltzmann law:** H = eσAT⁴ (σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴). **Wien's law:** λₘT = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K. Black surfaces absorb and emit best.

steps.title: Newton's law of cooling
steps.body:
Rate of loss of heat ∝ temperature difference with surroundings (for small differences): **dT/dt = −k(T − Tₛ)**.

Useful approximate form: (T₁ − T₂)/t = k[(T₁ + T₂)/2 − Tₛ].

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Glass window, K = 1 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, area 2 m², thickness 5 mm, ΔT = 10 K.
- H = 1 × 2 × 10/0.005 = **4000 W**

**Example 2:** The Sun's spectrum peaks near 500 nm. T = 2.9 × 10⁻³/5 × 10⁻⁷ ≈ **5800 K**.

**Example 3:** A body cools from 80 °C to 50 °C in 5 min in a 20 °C room. Time to cool from 60 °C to 30 °C?
- 30/5 = k(65 − 20) → k = 2/15 per min
- 30/t = (2/15)(45 − 20) = 10/3 → t = **9 min**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C in Stefan's law — use kelvin.
- Thinking radiation needs a medium.
- Applying Newton's law of cooling for very large temperature differences.

activity.prompt: Match the example to the mode of heat transfer
pairs: Room heater warming air in a room

quiz.q: Heat from the Sun reaches us by
quiz.why: Heat from the Sun travels across space (nearly a vacuum) by radiation, since conduction and convection need a medium.

quiz.q: If a body's absolute temperature doubles, radiated power becomes
quiz.why: By Stefan's law, radiated power is proportional to T⁴. Doubling T makes it 2⁴ = 16 times.

quiz.q: Wien's law relates
quiz.why: Wien's displacement law says λₘT = constant, relating the peak wavelength to the temperature of a body.

quiz.q: Cooking pots often have copper bottoms because copper
quiz.why: Copper has high thermal conductivity, so it spreads heat quickly and evenly across the base of a pot.

quiz.q: Newton's law of cooling: rate of cooling ∝
quiz.why: Newton's law of cooling says the rate of cooling is proportional to the temperature difference between the body and its surroundings, T − Tₛ.

questions.q: 0 K corresponds to
questions.why: Absolute zero, 0 K, is −273.15 °C, the lowest possible temperature.

questions.q: SI unit of thermal conductivity
questions.why: From H = KAΔT/L, K = HL/(AΔT), so the unit is W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.

questions.q: Lakes freeze from the top because
questions.why: Water is densest at 4 °C, so cooled water sinks until the lake reaches 4 °C, and then colder, lighter water stays on top and freezes first.

questions.q: 50 °C in °F
Assertion: Food cooks faster in a pressure cooker. Reason: Boiling point of water rises with pressure.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Water boils at a higher temperature under the raised pressure inside a pressure cooker (above 100 °C), so food cooks faster. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: β for a solid with α = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹
questions.why: For a solid the area expansion coefficient is twice the linear one: β = 2α = 2 × 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ = 3 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹. The volume coefficient γ would be 3α.

questions.q: A 1 m brass rod (α = 2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹) is heated by 100 K. Increase in length:
Case: 100 g of water at 90 °C is mixed with 300 g at 10 °C (no loss). Final temperature:
questions.why: Heat lost by the hot water = heat gained by the cold water: 100(90 − T) = 300(T − 10). So 9000 − 100T = 300T − 3000, giving 400T = 12000 and T = 30 °C.

questions.q: Two stars peak at 400 nm and 600 nm. Ratio of their surface temperatures (first : second):
questions.why: By Wien's law, λₘT is constant, so T ∝ 1/λₘ. The ratio of temperatures is 1/400 : 1/600 = 600 : 400 = 3 : 2.

questions.q: Heat needed to convert 10 g ice at 0 °C into water at 50 °C (L_f = 336 J/g, c = 4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹):
questions.why: Melting needs 10 g × 336 J/g = 3360 J. Then warming the 10 g of water from 0 to 50 °C needs 10 × 4.2 × 50 = 2100 J. Total = 3360 + 2100 = 5460 J.

questions.q: Two rods of equal length and area, conductivities K and 2K, are joined in series. Equivalent conductivity:
questions.why: For two rods in series, the total resistance adds: 2L/(K_eq A) = L/(KA) + L/(2KA) = 3L/(2KA). So K_eq = 4K/3.

questions.q: A body cools from 70 °C to 50 °C in 6 min in a 30 °C room. Using the average form, time to cool from 50 °C to 40 °C is about
questions.why: Using the average temperature: cooling rate 20/6 = k(60 − 30) gives k = 1/9 per min. For 50 to 40 °C, average temperature is 45 °C, so 10/t = (1/9)(45 − 30) = 15/9, giving t = 6 min.

questions.q: A steel scale is correct at 20 °C. At 40 °C it measures a length as 50 cm. True length (α = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹):
questions.why: At 40 °C the steel scale has expanded, so each mark spans more than its labelled length. The true length is therefore larger: 50(1 + 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ × 20) = 50 × 1.00024 = 50.012 cm.

questions.q: 5 g of steam at 100 °C condenses and cools to 20 °C. Heat released (L_v = 2260 J/g, c = 4.2):
questions.why: Condensation releases 5 g × 2260 J/g = 11300 J. Then cooling the water from 100 to 20 °C releases 5 × 4.2 × 80 = 1680 J. Total = 11300 + 1680 = 12980 J.

questions.q: Temperature of a black body is doubled. Wavelength of peak emission
questions.why: By Wien's law λₘT is constant. If T doubles, the peak wavelength halves.

questions.q: Convection does NOT occur in
questions.why: Convection needs bulk motion of a fluid (liquid or gas). In solids the particles cannot flow, so heat moves by conduction instead.

courses.title: Ch 11 · Thermodynamics
courses.summary: Thermal equilibrium and the zeroth law, heat, work and internal energy, the first law, specific heats of gases, thermodynamic processes, the second law, heat engines, refrigerators and the Carnot engine.
outcomes: Learners can state and apply the zeroth and first laws
Learners can calculate work in isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric and isochoric processes
Learners can relate Cₚ and C_v (Mayer's relation)

lessons.title: Zeroth law, heat, work and internal energy

scenes.text: A doctor waits a minute before reading the thermometer under your tongue.
She is waiting for thermal equilibrium — the zeroth law is why thermometers work at all.

steps.title: Zeroth law
steps.body: If A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This defines **temperature** as the property that is equal for bodies in equilibrium.

steps.title: Heat, work and internal energy
steps.body:
- **Internal energy U:** sum of molecular kinetic and potential energies; a **state variable** (depends only on the state, not on the path). For an ideal gas U depends only on T.
- **Heat Q** and **work W** are modes of energy transfer, NOT state variables — they depend on the process.
- Work done BY a gas: W = ∫P dV = area under the P–V curve.
- Sign convention (NCERT): Q positive when heat is supplied to the system; W positive when work is done BY the system.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A gas expands at constant pressure 2 × 10⁵ Pa from 1 L to 3 L.
- W = PΔV = 2 × 10⁵ × 2 × 10⁻³ = **400 J** (by the gas)

**Example 2:** On a P–V diagram a gas goes A → B along two different paths. Is ΔU the same? **Yes** (state variable). Is W the same? **No** (different areas).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a body 'contains heat' — it contains internal energy; heat is energy in transit.
- Using litres in PΔV without converting to m³ (1 L = 10⁻³ m³).
- Mixing sign conventions between books (chemistry often uses W on the system).

activity.prompt: State variable or path-dependent?

quiz.q: The zeroth law leads to the concept of
quiz.why: The zeroth law states that bodies in thermal equilibrium with a third body are in equilibrium with each other, which leads to the concept of temperature.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a state variable?
quiz.why: Heat Q depends on the path of the process, so it is not a state variable. U, T and P depend only on the state of the system.

quiz.q: Work by a gas equals the area under the
quiz.why: Work done by a gas is W = ∫P dV, the area under the curve on a P–V diagram.

quiz.q: For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on
quiz.why: An ideal gas has no intermolecular forces, so its internal energy is only the kinetic energy of its molecules, which depends only on temperature.

quiz.q: Gas expands from 2 L to 5 L at 10⁵ Pa. Work done:
quiz.why: At constant pressure, W = PΔV = 10⁵ Pa × (5 − 2) × 10⁻³ m³ = 300 J. Litres must be converted to m³.

lessons.title: First law and specific heats of gases

scenes.text: Pumping a tyre quickly, Rahul feels the pump barrel heat up.
Work done on the air raises its internal energy — the first law of thermodynamics.

steps.title: First law
steps.body: **ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW** — energy conservation including heat. Heat supplied goes into raising internal energy and doing external work.

steps.title: Specific heats and Mayer's relation
steps.body:
- Constant volume: ΔW = 0, so ΔQ = ΔU = nC_vΔT.
- Constant pressure: ΔQ = nCₚΔT = ΔU + PΔV.
- For an ideal gas PΔV = nRΔT → **Cₚ − C_v = R** (Mayer's relation), R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
- γ = Cₚ/C_v: monatomic 5/3, diatomic 7/5 (at room temperature).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A gas absorbs 500 J and does 200 J of work. ΔU = 500 − 200 = **300 J**.

**Example 2:** 2 mol of a diatomic ideal gas is heated by 10 K at constant pressure.
- W = nRΔT = 2 × 8.314 × 10 = **166 J**
- ΔU = nC_vΔT = 2 × (5/2 × 8.314) × 10 = **416 J**
- Q = 166 + 416 = **582 J** (= nCₚΔT ✓)

**Example 3:** In a cyclic process ΔU = 0, so net Q = net W.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wrong signs: work done ON the gas is negative ΔW in this convention.
- Using Cₚ for ΔU — ΔU = nC_vΔT for ANY process of an ideal gas.
- Forgetting that ΔU = 0 only for isothermal (ideal gas) or cyclic processes.

activity.prompt: A gas is given 800 J of heat and 300 J of work is done ON it. Change in internal energy (J)?

quiz.q: First law of thermodynamics is a form of
quiz.why: The first law, ΔU = Q − W, is the principle of conservation of energy, with heat included as a form of energy.

quiz.q: Cₚ − C_v for an ideal gas equals
quiz.why: For an ideal gas, Mayer's relation says Cp − Cv = R.

quiz.q: γ for a monatomic gas
quiz.why: For a monatomic gas Cv = 3R/2 and Cp = 5R/2, so γ = Cp/Cv = 5/3 ≈ 1.67.

quiz.q: In an isochoric process, work done is
quiz.why: An isochoric process has constant volume, so ΔV = 0 and work done (PΔV) is zero.

quiz.q: A gas does 150 J work with no heat exchange. ΔU =
quiz.why: With no heat exchange, Q = 0, so ΔU = Q − W = 0 − 150 = −150 J. The gas does work using its own internal energy.

scenes.text: A truck's diesel engine has no spark plug.
Rapid (adiabatic) compression heats the air so much that injected fuel ignites by itself.

steps.title: Quasi-static processes
steps.body:
Processes slow enough that the system stays near equilibrium.
- **Isothermal** (T const): PV = const; ΔU = 0 → Q = W = **nRT ln(V₂/V₁)**.
- **Adiabatic** (Q = 0): **PV^γ = const**, TV^(γ−1) = const; W = (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(γ − 1) = nR(T₁ − T₂)/(γ − 1). Expansion cools the gas; compression heats it.
- **Isochoric** (V const): W = 0, Q = ΔU.
- **Isobaric** (P const): W = PΔV = nRΔT.
- **Cyclic:** ΔU = 0, Q_net = W_net = area enclosed by the cycle on P–V.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** 1 mol ideal gas expands isothermally at 300 K to twice its volume.
- W = 8.314 × 300 × ln 2 ≈ **1729 J**; Q = 1729 J; ΔU = 0

**Example 2:** Air (γ = 1.4) at 300 K is compressed adiabatically to 1/8 of its volume.
- T₂ = T₁(V₁/V₂)^(γ−1) = 300 × 8^0.4 ≈ 300 × 2.30 ≈ **690 K**

**Example 3:** An adiabatic curve is steeper than an isothermal one on P–V: slopes −γP/V vs −P/V.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing PV = const for adiabatic processes.
- Thinking adiabatic means constant temperature.
- Using log₁₀ where ln is needed (ln x = 2.303 log₁₀ x).

activity.prompt: Match the process to its key property

quiz.q: In an adiabatic expansion, gas temperature
quiz.why: In an adiabatic expansion no heat enters, so the gas does work at the expense of its internal energy, and its temperature falls.

quiz.q: Isothermal work for an ideal gas
quiz.why: For an ideal gas expanding isothermally, W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁).

quiz.q: Equation for an adiabatic process
quiz.why: With Q = 0 in the first law for an ideal gas, you get PV^γ = constant for an adiabatic process.

quiz.q: In a cyclic process, net work equals
quiz.why: In a cycle the gas returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0 and net work equals net heat. Net work is the area enclosed by the loop on a P–V diagram.

quiz.q: On a P–V diagram, the adiabatic is
quiz.why: On a P–V diagram an adiabatic curve is steeper than an isotherm, since its slope is γ times that of the isothermal curve, and γ > 1.

lessons.title: Second law, heat engines, refrigerators and the Carnot engine

story.title: Why can't a ship run on sea heat?

scenes.text: The ocean holds enormous internal energy. Why can't a ship just use it to run its engines?
The second law: an engine needs a colder reservoir to dump heat into. Heat alone, at one temperature, cannot be fully turned into work.

steps.title: Heat engines and refrigerators
steps.body:
- **Heat engine:** takes Q₁ from a hot reservoir, does work W, rejects Q₂ to a cold one. Efficiency **η = W/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁**.
- **Refrigerator/heat pump:** work W moves heat Q₂ from cold to hot. **Coefficient of performance** α = Q₂/W = Q₂/(Q₁ − Q₂).

steps.title: Second law
steps.body:
- **Kelvin–Planck:** no process is possible whose sole result is absorption of heat from a reservoir and complete conversion into work (no 100% efficient engine).
- **Clausius:** no process is possible whose sole result is transfer of heat from a colder to a hotter body.
- **Reversible** processes can be retraced exactly with no net change in surroundings (idealised, quasi-static, no friction). Real processes (free expansion, friction, heat flow across finite ΔT) are irreversible.

steps.title: Carnot engine
steps.body: A reversible engine between T₁ and T₂ using two isothermals and two adiabatics. **η = 1 − T₂/T₁** — the maximum possible between those temperatures (Carnot's theorem), independent of working substance. For a Carnot refrigerator α = T₂/(T₁ − T₂).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Carnot engine between 500 K and 300 K: η = 1 − 300/500 = **40%**.

**Example 2:** An engine takes 1000 J and rejects 600 J per cycle: W = 400 J, η = **40%**.

**Example 3:** A refrigerator keeps food at 0 °C (273 K) in a 30 °C (303 K) room. Ideal COP = 273/30 ≈ **9.1**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C in Carnot formulas — always kelvin.
- Thinking efficiency can reach 100% if friction is removed.
- Confusing COP (can be > 1) with efficiency (always < 1).

activity.prompt: A Carnot engine works between 627 °C and 27 °C. What is its efficiency in percent?

quiz.q: Efficiency of a Carnot engine depends on
quiz.why: A Carnot engine's efficiency η = 1 − T₂/T₁ depends only on the temperatures of the source and sink, not on the working substance.

quiz.q: Which statement says a perfect refrigerator is impossible?
quiz.why: The Clausius statement says heat cannot flow from a colder to a hotter body by itself without work, so a perfect refrigerator is impossible. The Kelvin–Planck statement concerns engines.

quiz.q: Free expansion of a gas is
quiz.why: Free expansion into a vacuum cannot reverse itself without outside intervention, so it is an irreversible process.

quiz.q: An engine absorbs 800 J and does 200 J work. Efficiency:
quiz.why: Efficiency = work done/heat absorbed = 200/800 = 0.25 = 25%.

quiz.q: Carnot efficiency becomes 100% only if
quiz.why: η = 1 − T₂/T₁ is 1 only if T₂ = 0 K (or T₁ is infinite). A sink at absolute zero cannot be reached in practice.

sources: NCERT Physics Class 11 (topic: second law, Carnot engine)

questions.q: Which law defines temperature?
questions.why: The zeroth law of thermodynamics, about thermal equilibrium, gives the definition of temperature.

questions.q: In an isothermal process for an ideal gas, ΔU is
questions.why: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature. In an isothermal process the temperature is constant, so ΔU = 0.

questions.q: γ for a diatomic gas at room temperature
questions.why: A diatomic gas at room temperature has 5 degrees of freedom, so γ = 1 + 2/5 = 7/5 = 1.4.

questions.q: A gas gets 400 J heat and does 150 J work. ΔU:
questions.why: By the first law, ΔU = Q − W = 400 − 150 = 250 J.

questions.q: Assertion: No heat engine can be 100% efficient. Reason: Some heat must be rejected to a colder reservoir.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. By the Kelvin–Planck statement, an engine must reject some heat to a colder reservoir, so it cannot convert all absorbed heat into work.

questions.q: Work done in a constant-volume process
questions.why: Constant volume means ΔV = 0, so the work done (PΔV) is zero.

questions.q: Carnot engine with sink at 27 °C has efficiency 50%. Source temperature:
questions.why: The sink is 27 °C = 300 K. 1 − 300/T₁ = 0.5 gives T₁ = 600 K (not in °C).

questions.q: Case: A refrigerator extracts 600 J from the freezer using 200 J of electrical work per cycle. COP and heat rejected to the room:
questions.why: COP = heat extracted/work = 600/200 = 3. Heat rejected to the room = 600 + 200 = 800 J (energy conservation).

questions.q: 3 mol of ideal gas at 400 K expands isothermally from 10 L to 20 L. Work done (ln 2 = 0.693):
questions.why: For an isothermal expansion W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁) = 3 × 8.314 × 400 × 0.693 ≈ 6914 J ≈ 6.9 kJ.

questions.q: A monatomic gas (γ = 5/3) is compressed adiabatically to 1/8 of its volume. Pressure increases by a factor
questions.why: For an adiabatic change P₂/P₁ = (V₁/V₂)^γ = 8^(5/3) = (2³)^(5/3) = 2⁵ = 32.

questions.q: For 1 mol monatomic gas heated at constant pressure by 20 K, heat supplied is about (R = 8.31)
questions.why: At constant pressure, Q = nCpΔT with Cp = 5R/2 for a monatomic gas: 2.5 × 8.31 × 20 ≈ 416 J.

questions.q: Efficiency of a Carnot engine is 1/6. On lowering the sink temperature by 62 K it becomes 1/3. Source temperature:
questions.why: Efficiency 1/6 means T₂/T₁ = 5/6. With the sink lowered by 62 K, (T₂ − 62)/T₁ = 2/3. Subtracting gives 62/T₁ = 5/6 − 2/3 = 1/6, so T₁ = 372 K.

questions.q: Ideal gas in a cycle absorbs 500 J and rejects 300 J. Net work and ΔU:
questions.why: In a cycle ΔU = 0. Net work = heat absorbed − heat rejected = 500 − 300 = 200 J.

questions.q: Air at 27 °C (γ = 1.4) is suddenly compressed to 1/32 of its volume. Final temperature (32^0.4 = 4):
questions.why: For an adiabatic change TV^(γ−1) is constant, so T₂ = T₁(V₁/V₂)^0.4 = 300 × 32^0.4 = 300 × 4 = 1200 K (27 °C = 300 K).

questions.q: COP of an ideal refrigerator between −3 °C and 27 °C:
questions.why: For an ideal refrigerator COP = T_cold/(T_hot − T_cold) = 270/(300 − 270) = 270/30 = 9, with temperatures in kelvin.

questions.q: Internal energy of an ideal gas is a function of
questions.why: There are no intermolecular forces in an ideal gas, so there is no potential energy, and internal energy depends only on temperature.

courses.summary: Molecular nature of matter, ideal gas equation, kinetic-theory derivation of pressure, kinetic interpretation of temperature, rms speed, equipartition of energy, specific heats and mean free path.
outcomes: Learners can use PV = nRT = Nk_BT and the gas laws
Learners can derive P = (1/3)nm⟨v²⟩ and relate temperature to mean KE
Learners can compute rms speeds

lessons.title: Molecular nature of matter and the ideal gas law

scenes.text: A balloon left in a parked car on a hot day looks tighter in the afternoon.
At constant volume-ish, pressure rises with temperature — the gas laws in everyday life.

steps.title: Ideal gas equation
steps.body:
- **PV = nRT = Nk_BT**, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
- **Boyle's law** (T const): PV = const.
- **Charles' law** (P const): V ∝ T.
- **Dalton's law** of partial pressures: P = P₁ + P₂ + … for non-reacting ideal gases.
- 1 mol of an ideal gas at STP (273 K, 1 atm) occupies about 22.4 L.

Real gases approach ideal behaviour at low pressure and high temperature.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A gas at 2 atm occupies 3 L. At constant T, its volume at 6 atm = 2 × 3/6 = **1 L**.

**Example 2:** An oxygen cylinder of 30 L at 27 °C has 15 atm pressure. Moles: n = PV/RT = 15 × 1.013 × 10⁵ × 0.03/(8.314 × 300) ≈ **18.3 mol**.

**Example 3:** Number of molecules in 1 m³ of gas at STP: n = P/(k_BT) = 1.013 × 10⁵/(1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 273) ≈ **2.7 × 10²⁵ m⁻³**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C instead of K in gas laws.
- Mixing litres and m³ with R = 8.314 (use SI or R = 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ consistently).
- Applying ideal gas law at very high pressure without caution.

activity.prompt: A gas at 300 K and constant pressure is heated until its volume doubles. What is its new temperature in K?

quiz.q: Boltzmann constant k_B equals
quiz.why: The Boltzmann constant is the gas constant per molecule: k_B = R/N_A.

quiz.q: Boyle's law holds at constant
quiz.why: Boyle's law says that for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, PV is constant.

quiz.q: Molar volume at STP is about
quiz.why: One mole of any ideal gas at STP occupies about 22.4 litres.

quiz.q: Real gases behave most ideally at
quiz.why: Real gases behave most like ideal gases at low pressure and high temperature, when molecules are far apart and move fast so intermolecular forces matter little.

quiz.q: Total pressure of a mixture of non-reacting gases equals the sum of partial pressures — this is
quiz.why: Dalton's law of partial pressures says the total pressure of a mixture of non-reacting gases equals the sum of the partial pressures.

lessons.title: Pressure from kinetic theory and meaning of temperature

scenes.text: Steady rain on an umbrella feels like a constant push, though it is millions of tiny impacts.
Gas pressure on a wall is the same idea: countless molecular collisions averaged into a steady force.

steps.title: Assumptions and derivation
steps.body:
Assumptions: many identical molecules, negligible size, elastic collisions, no forces except during collisions, random motion.

A molecule with velocity component vₓ hitting a wall transfers 2mvₓ. Number hitting area A in time Δt with speed vₓ is ½ n A vₓ Δt (half move toward the wall). Pressure = n m ⟨vₓ²⟩. By isotropy ⟨vₓ²⟩ = ⟨v²⟩/3:
**P = (1/3) n m ⟨v²⟩ = (1/3) ρ ⟨v²⟩**

steps.title: Kinetic interpretation of temperature
steps.body:
PV = (2/3) N × (½m⟨v²⟩). Comparing with PV = Nk_BT:
- **Average translational KE per molecule = (3/2) k_BT**
- **v_rms = √(3k_BT/m) = √(3RT/M)** (M = molar mass in kg/mol)

Temperature is a measure of the average molecular kinetic energy. At the same T, lighter molecules move faster: v_rms ∝ 1/√M.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** v_rms of O₂ at 300 K: √(3 × 8.314 × 300/0.032) = √233,800 ≈ **484 m/s**.

**Example 2:** Ratio v_rms(H₂)/v_rms(O₂) at the same T = √(32/2) = **4**.

**Example 3:** Average KE of a gas molecule at 300 K = 1.5 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300 ≈ **6.2 × 10⁻²¹ J**, independent of the gas.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using M in g/mol in √(3RT/M) — convert to kg/mol.
- Saying heavier gases have more KE at the same T — average KE depends only on T.
- Confusing v_rms with average speed or most probable speed (v_mp < v_avg < v_rms).

activity.prompt: At what temperature (K) will v_rms of a gas be double its value at 300 K?

quiz.q: Pressure from kinetic theory P =
quiz.why: The kinetic theory result is P = (1/3)ρ⟨v²⟩, where ρ is the gas density and ⟨v²⟩ is the mean square speed.

quiz.q: Average KE per molecule
quiz.why: The average translational kinetic energy per molecule is (3/2)k_BT.

quiz.q: v_rms ∝
quiz.why: v_rms = √(3RT/M), so it is proportional to √T.

quiz.q: At the same T, which has the highest v_rms?
quiz.why: v_rms ∝ 1/√M. At the same temperature the lightest molecule, hydrogen, moves fastest.

quiz.q: If T is fixed and M becomes 4 times, v_rms becomes
quiz.why: Since v_rms ∝ 1/√M, making M four times larger halves v_rms.

lessons.title: Equipartition of energy and specific heats

scenes.text: Helium and nitrogen at the same temperature need different heat to warm by 1 K per mole.
Nitrogen molecules can rotate as well as move; their energy spreads over more 'degrees of freedom'.

steps.title: Degrees of freedom and equipartition
steps.body:
- **Degrees of freedom (f):** independent ways a molecule can store energy. Monatomic: 3 translational. Rigid diatomic: 3 translational + 2 rotational = 5. Vibrational modes add 2 each (KE + PE) at high temperature.
- **Law of equipartition:** in thermal equilibrium each quadratic energy term contributes ½k_BT per molecule.
- So U per mole = (f/2)RT → **C_v = (f/2)R, Cₚ = C_v + R, γ = 1 + 2/f**.

steps.title: Standard values
steps.body:
- Monatomic (He, Ar): C_v = 3R/2, Cₚ = 5R/2, γ = 5/3
- Rigid diatomic (O₂, N₂): C_v = 5R/2, Cₚ = 7R/2, γ = 7/5
- Diatomic with vibration: C_v = 7R/2, γ = 9/7
- Non-linear polyatomic (rigid): f = 6, C_v = 3R, γ = 4/3
- **Solids (Dulong–Petit):** C ≈ 3R ≈ 25 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (each atom oscillates in 3D: 6 quadratic terms)
- Water: about 75 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (~9R).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A mixture of 1 mol He and 1 mol O₂ (rigid). C_v(mix) = (3R/2 + 5R/2)/2 = **2R**; Cₚ = 3R; γ = **1.5**.

**Example 2:** Internal energy of 2 mol N₂ at 300 K = 2 × (5/2) × 8.314 × 300 ≈ **12.5 kJ**.

**Example 3:** γ for a gas with f = 7: 1 + 2/7 = **9/7 ≈ 1.29**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting vibrational modes count twice (kinetic and potential).
- Averaging γ directly for mixtures — average C_v and Cₚ by moles first.
- Applying classical equipartition at very low temperatures (quantum effects freeze modes).

activity.prompt: Match the molecule type to γ

quiz.q: Degrees of freedom of a rigid diatomic molecule
quiz.why: A rigid diatomic molecule has 3 translational and 2 rotational degrees of freedom, giving 5.

quiz.q: Each degree of freedom contributes energy
quiz.why: By the law of equipartition, each degree of freedom contributes ½k_BT of energy per molecule.

quiz.q: Dulong–Petit value for molar heat of solids
quiz.why: The Dulong–Petit law says the molar heat capacity of solids is about 3R (≈ 25 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹), from 6 quadratic energy terms per atom.

quiz.q: C_v of a monatomic ideal gas
quiz.why: A monatomic gas has f = 3 degrees of freedom, so Cv = (f/2)R = 3R/2.

lessons.title: Mean free path

scenes.text: Molecules move at hundreds of m/s, yet perfume takes many seconds to cross a room.
Each molecule collides billions of times a second and zig-zags — its mean free path is tiny.

steps.title: Definition and formula
steps.body:
The **mean free path** λ is the average distance a molecule travels between collisions.
**λ = 1/(√2 π d² n)** where d = molecular diameter, n = number density.
- λ ∝ 1/n: larger at low pressure (λ ∝ T/P at fixed d).
- Collision frequency ≈ v̄/λ.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Nitrogen at STP: n ≈ 2.7 × 10²⁵ m⁻³, d ≈ 3 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.
- λ = 1/(1.414 × 3.14 × 9 × 10⁻²⁰ × 2.7 × 10²⁵) ≈ **9.3 × 10⁻⁸ m (about 0.1 µm)** — roughly 300 molecular diameters.

**Example 2:** If pressure is halved at constant T, λ **doubles**.

**Example 3:** With v̄ ≈ 500 m/s and λ ≈ 10⁻⁷ m, collision frequency ≈ **5 × 10⁹ s⁻¹**.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Vacuum tubes, electron microscopes and particle accelerators need very low pressure so the mean free path becomes longer than the apparatus. Slow diffusion of smells and gases in still air is also explained by short mean free paths.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using radius instead of diameter in λ.
- Thinking λ grows with molecular size (it falls as 1/d²).
- Forgetting the √2 factor from relative motion.

statements.s: Mean free path increases as pressure decreases (constant T).
Bigger molecules have longer mean free paths.
At STP the mean free path in air is about 0.1 µm.
Diffusion is slow because molecules move slowly.
statements.why: They move fast but collide very often.

quiz.q: Mean free path is inversely proportional to
quiz.why: The mean free path is λ = 1/(√2 π d² n), so it is inversely proportional to d², the square of the molecular diameter.

quiz.q: Doubling the number density makes λ
quiz.why: Since λ ∝ 1/n, doubling the number density halves the mean free path.

quiz.q: Order of λ for air at STP
quiz.why: For air at STP, the mean free path is about 10⁻⁷ m (roughly 0.1 µm), much larger than a molecular diameter.

quiz.q: Vacuum in an electron gun is needed to
quiz.why: A vacuum reduces the number of gas molecules, so the mean free path of electrons becomes longer and they have fewer collisions.

quiz.q: Collision frequency ≈
quiz.why: Collision frequency is the average speed divided by the mean free path (distance between collisions): v̄/λ.

v_rms of N₂ at 300 K (M = 0.028 kg/mol) is about

questions.why: Helium has Cv = 3R/2 and rigid N₂ has 5R/2. The mixture's Cv = (2 × 3/2 + 1 × 5/2)R/3 = (3 + 2.5)R/3 = 11R/6.

questions.q: Pressure of a gas is P = (1/3)ρ⟨v²⟩. Gas density 1.25 kg/m³ at 10⁵ Pa. v_rms:
Mean free path at 1 atm is λ. At 0.01 atm and the same T it is
questions.why: At fixed temperature, λ ∝ 1/n ∝ 1/P. Lowering the pressure to 1/100 makes the mean free path 100 times longer.

questions.q: Temperature at which v_rms of O₂ equals that of H₂ at 300 K:
questions.why: v_rms ∝ √(T/M). For equal speeds, T/M must be equal: T/32 = 300/2, so T = 300 × 16 = 4800 K.

questions.q: For a gas γ = 1.4. Fraction of heat supplied at constant pressure that goes into internal energy:
questions.why: At constant pressure the heat supplied is nCpΔT and the part going into internal energy is nCvΔT. The fraction is Cv/Cp = 1/γ = 1/1.4 = 5/7.

questions.q: Which assumption is NOT part of kinetic theory?
options: Molecules attract strongly at all distances
questions.why: Kinetic theory assumes there are no intermolecular forces except during collisions. Strong attraction at all distances contradicts that assumption.

courses.title: Ch 13 · Oscillations
courses.summary: Periodic and oscillatory motion, simple harmonic motion and its equations, velocity and acceleration in SHM, the force law, energy in SHM, the spring–mass system and the simple pendulum.
outcomes: Learners can describe SHM with x = A cos(ωt + φ)
Learners can find velocity, acceleration and energy at any displacement
Learners can derive periods of spring–mass systems and the simple pendulum
Learners can combine springs and analyse simple SHM variations

scenes.text: A courtyard swing goes back and forth, each swing taking the same time.
Its position plotted against time looks like a cosine curve — the signature of simple harmonic motion.

steps.title: Terms
steps.body:
- **Periodic motion** repeats after a fixed time T (period). Frequency ν = 1/T (Hz).
- **Oscillatory motion:** periodic to-and-fro motion about a mean position.
- **SHM:** x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ)
  - A = amplitude, (ωt + φ) = phase, φ = phase constant
  - **ω = 2π/T = 2πν** (angular frequency)
- SHM is the projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** x = 5 cos(2πt + π/4) cm.
- A = **5 cm**, ω = 2π rad/s → T = **1 s**, ν = 1 Hz, φ = π/4
- At t = 0: x = 5 cos 45° ≈ **3.54 cm**

**Example 2:** Is sin ωt + cos ωt SHM? = √2 sin(ωt + π/4) → **yes**, amplitude √2, period 2π/ω.

**Example 3:** Is e^(−ωt) periodic? **No** — it never repeats.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking every periodic motion is SHM (a bouncing ball is periodic but not SHM).
- Confusing ω (rad/s) with ν (Hz).
- Forgetting the calculator must be in radians for phase.

activity.prompt: Classify each motion

items.text: A ball bouncing elastically on the floor

quiz.q: Angular frequency of SHM with T = 0.5 s
quiz.why: Angular frequency ω = 2π/T = 2π/0.5 = 4π rad/s.

quiz.q: In x = A cos(ωt + φ), A is
quiz.why: In x = A cos(ωt + φ), A is the amplitude, the maximum displacement from the mean position.

quiz.q: SHM is the projection of
quiz.why: SHM can be seen as the projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter of the reference circle.

quiz.q: Frequency of a motion with period 0.02 s
quiz.why: Frequency is the reciprocal of period: ν = 1/T = 1/0.02 = 50 Hz.

quiz.q: sin ωt − cos ωt represents
quiz.why: sin ωt − cos ωt = √2 sin(ωt − π/4), a sinusoid with amplitude √2. So it is SHM with amplitude √2.

lessons.title: Velocity, acceleration, force law and energy in SHM

scenes.text: When a bike goes over a bump, the spring compresses and bounces.
Energy keeps switching between spring PE and kinetic energy — total staying constant in ideal SHM.

steps.title: Kinematics of SHM
steps.body:
From x = A cos(ωt + φ):
- v = −Aω sin(ωt + φ); in terms of x: **v = ω√(A² − x²)**; v_max = Aω at the mean position
- **a = −ω²x**; a_max = Aω² at the extremes

**Force law:** F = ma = −mω²x = **−kx** with k = mω² → ω = √(k/m). A restoring force proportional to displacement always gives SHM.

steps.title: Energy
steps.body:
- KE = ½mω²(A² − x²) = ½k(A² − x²)
- PE = ½kx²
- **Total E = ½kA² = ½mω²A²** (constant)
- KE = PE when x = A/√2.
- Both KE and PE oscillate with frequency 2ν.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** For x = 5 cos(2πt) cm: v_max = 5 × 2π = **10π cm/s ≈ 31.4 cm/s**; a_max = 5 × 4π² ≈ **197 cm/s²**.

**Example 2:** k = 200 N/m, A = 0.1 m. Total energy = ½ × 200 × 0.01 = **1 J**. At x = 0.05 m: PE = 0.25 J, KE = **0.75 J**.

**Example 3:** A particle in SHM has v = 3 cm/s at x = 4 cm and v = 4 cm/s at x = 3 cm. Then 9 = ω²(A² − 16), 16 = ω²(A² − 9) → subtract: 7 = 7ω² → ω = 1 rad/s, A = **5 cm**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking acceleration is maximum at the mean position (it is zero there).
- Forgetting the minus sign in a = −ω²x (it points toward the mean).
- Saying energy frequency equals oscillation frequency (it is double).

activity.label: Displacement as a fraction of amplitude (x/A)

bands.text: Mean position: all energy kinetic, speed maximum, acceleration zero.
Extreme: all energy potential, speed zero, acceleration maximum.

quiz.q: Speed in SHM is maximum at
quiz.why: In SHM v = ω√(A² − x²), which is greatest at x = 0, the mean position.

quiz.q: Acceleration in SHM is proportional to
quiz.why: In SHM, a = −ω²x: the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and opposite in direction.

quiz.q: Total energy of SHM is proportional to
quiz.why: The total energy in SHM is ½kA², so it is proportional to the square of the amplitude.

quiz.q: KE equals PE at
quiz.why: KE equals PE when ½k(A² − x²) = ½kx², so x² = A²/2 and x = A/√2.

quiz.q: If SHM frequency is ν, KE oscillates with frequency
quiz.why: KE is proportional to sin² (or cos²) of ωt, which repeats twice as often as the displacement. So KE oscillates at 2ν.

sources: NCERT Physics Class 11 (topic: energy in SHM)

lessons.title: Spring–mass system and simple pendulum

scenes.text: Grandfather's pendulum clock runs slow every summer.
Heat lengthens the pendulum rod; since T = 2π√(l/g), a longer pendulum ticks slower.

steps.title: Spring–mass system
steps.body:
F = −kx → ω = √(k/m), **T = 2π√(m/k)** (independent of amplitude and of g for a vertical spring — g only shifts the equilibrium).
- Springs in **parallel:** k = k₁ + k₂
- Springs in **series:** 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂
- Cutting a spring into n equal parts makes each part n times stiffer.

steps.title: Simple pendulum (derivation)
steps.body:
Bob of mass m on a light string of length L. Restoring torque about the support: τ = −mgL sin θ. With I = mL² and α = d²θ/dt²:
mL² α = −mgL sin θ → for small θ (sin θ ≈ θ): α = −(g/L)θ → SHM with ω = √(g/L).
**T = 2π√(L/g)** — independent of mass and (for small angles) of amplitude.

**Seconds pendulum:** T = 2 s → L = gT²/4π² ≈ 0.993 m (≈ 1 m).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** m = 1 kg, k = 100 N/m. T = 2π√(0.01) = 2π/10 ≈ **0.628 s**.

**Example 2:** Length of a seconds pendulum (g = 9.8): L = 9.8 × 4/(4π²) ≈ **0.993 m**.

**Example 3:** A pendulum is taken to the Moon (g/6). T becomes **√6 ≈ 2.45 times** longer.

**Example 4:** Two springs of 100 N/m each: parallel k = 200 N/m; series k = 50 N/m. With 2 kg: T_parallel = 2π√(0.01) ≈ 0.63 s; T_series = 2π√(0.04) ≈ 1.26 s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a heavier bob swings slower — T is independent of mass.
- Using T = 2π√(L/g) for large angles.
- Measuring L to the top of the bob instead of to its centre.

activity.prompt: A pendulum of length 2.45 m swings where g = 9.8 m/s². What is its period in seconds? (use π = 3.14)

quiz.q: Period of a simple pendulum depends on
quiz.why: For a simple pendulum T = 2π√(L/g), which depends on the length and g, not on the mass of the bob (for small amplitudes).

quiz.q: Length of a pendulum is made 4 times. Period becomes
quiz.why: T ∝ √L. Making L four times as long multiplies T by √4 = 2.

quiz.q: Two springs k₁ and k₂ in series give
quiz.why: For springs in series 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂, so k = k₁k₂/(k₁ + k₂).

quiz.q: Mass on a spring: mass made 4 times. Period
quiz.why: T = 2π√(m/k) ∝ √m. With four times the mass, the period doubles.

quiz.q: A pendulum clock in a lift accelerating upward will
quiz.why: In an upward-accelerating lift the effective gravity is g + a, which is larger, so T = 2π√(L/g_eff) decreases and the clock runs fast.

sources: NCERT Physics Class 11 (topic: spring and pendulum)

lessons.title: Problem practice: identifying SHM and JEE bridge

scenes.text: Sahil pushes a floating bottle down and lets go — it bobs up and down.
Extra buoyancy is proportional to extra depth: a restoring force ∝ displacement. It's SHM again!

steps.title: Recipe for proving SHM
steps.body:
1. Displace the system by small x from equilibrium.
2. Find the net restoring force (or torque) F.
3. Show F = −(constant) × x.
4. Then ω = √(constant/m) (or √(constant/I) for rotation) and T = 2π/ω.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (floating cylinder):** Cross-section A, mass m, liquid density ρ. Pushing down by x adds buoyancy ρAgx → F = −(ρAg)x → **T = 2π√(m/(ρAg))**.

**Example 2 (liquid in U-tube):** Column of total length L. Displacing one side by x makes a height difference 2x: F = −(2Aρg)x, mass = AρL → **T = 2π√(L/2g)**.

**Example 3 (tunnel through Earth):** Inside a uniform Earth, g(r) = g r/R → a = −(g/R)r → T = 2π√(R/g) ≈ **84 min** (same as a low-orbit satellite).

steps.title: Damping and resonance (JEE bridge)
steps.body: Real oscillators lose energy to friction: amplitude decays (damped oscillations). Driven by a periodic force, an oscillator responds most strongly when the driving frequency is near its natural frequency — **resonance** (soldiers break step on bridges; tuning a radio).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the small-displacement approximation.
- Using total length instead of displaced length in U-tube problems.
- Using g at the surface for points inside the Earth.

activity.prompt: Order the steps for proving a motion is SHM
items: Displace the body slightly from equilibrium
Write the net restoring force or torque
Show it is proportional to displacement with a minus sign
Identify ω² = constant / mass (or / I)
Write T = 2π/ω

quiz.q: For a floating body bobbing vertically, the restoring force comes from
quiz.why: A body floating in a liquid gets a restoring force from the extra (or reduced) buoyant force when it is pushed down (or up), which is proportional to the displacement.

quiz.q: Period of liquid in a U-tube with column length L
quiz.why: If the liquid is displaced by y in one limb, the height difference is 2y, so the restoring force is 2ρAgy, giving T = 2π√(L/2g).

quiz.q: Resonance occurs when driving frequency
quiz.why: Resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals the system's natural frequency, giving the maximum amplitude response.

quiz.q: A body dropped into a tunnel through Earth's centre would
quiz.why: Inside the Earth the gravitational force on a body is proportional to its distance from the centre and directed toward it, which is the condition for SHM.

quiz.q: Damping causes
quiz.why: Damping removes energy from the oscillator, so the amplitude decays over time.

questions.q: Unit of angular frequency
questions.why: Angular frequency ω = 2πν is measured in radians per second.

questions.q: In SHM, acceleration is zero at
questions.why: Since a = −ω²x, the acceleration in SHM is zero where the displacement is zero, at the mean position.

questions.q: Period of a seconds pendulum
questions.why: A seconds pendulum takes 1 second for each swing, so its full period is 2 s.

questions.q: x = 3 sin(4t) m. Maximum speed
questions.why: For x = A sin ωt with A = 3 m and ω = 4 rad/s, the maximum speed is Aω = 3 × 4 = 12 m/s.

questions.q: Assertion: Period of a simple pendulum does not depend on the mass of the bob. Reason: Both the restoring force and the inertia are proportional to mass.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. For a pendulum, the restoring force (mg sin θ) and the inertia (m) are both proportional to m, so m cancels in T = 2π√(L/g).

questions.q: Spring of k = 400 N/m with 1 kg. Frequency:
questions.why: ω = √(k/m) = √400 = 20 rad/s. The frequency is ν = ω/2π = 20/6.28 ≈ 3.18 Hz.

questions.q: A particle in SHM has amplitude 4 cm. Speed is half its maximum at x =
questions.why: v = ω√(A² − x²) = ωA/2 gives √(A² − x²) = A/2, so x² = 3A²/4 and x = (√3/2)A = (√3/2) × 4 = 2√3 cm.

questions.q: Case: A clock pendulum is 1% too long. Roughly how many seconds does the clock lose per day (86400 s)?
questions.why: T ∝ √L, so a 1% longer pendulum has a period 0.5% longer. The clock loses 0.005 × 86400 = 432 s per day.

questions.q: Energy of a 0.5 kg mass in SHM with A = 0.2 m and ω = 10 rad/s:
questions.why: Energy = ½mω²A² = ½ × 0.5 × 100 × 0.04 = 1 J.

questions.q: A spring is cut into two equal halves. Each half's spring constant is (original k)
questions.why: A spring's stiffness is inversely proportional to its length, so halving the length doubles the spring constant: 2k.

questions.q: A 1 kg block between two springs k₁ = 100 N/m and k₂ = 300 N/m fixed to walls on either side. Period (π ≈ 3.14):
questions.why: A block between two springs attached to walls on both sides feels both springs together, so k_eff = 100 + 300 = 400 N/m. T = 2π√(1/400) = 2π/20 ≈ 0.314 s.

questions.q: A particle's displacement is x = 2 sin²(ωt). Its motion is
options: SHM with amplitude 1 about x = 1, frequency 2ω/2π
questions.why: 2 sin²ωt = 1 − cos 2ωt, which is SHM about x = 1 with amplitude 1 and angular frequency 2ω (frequency 2ω/2π).

questions.q: A pendulum's period on Earth is 2 s. On a planet with g' = g/4 it is
questions.why: T = 2π√(L/g) ∝ 1/√g. With g/4, T becomes √4 = 2 times as long: 2 × 2 = 4 s.

questions.q: A cylinder of mass 0.8 kg and cross-section 10 cm² floats upright in water. Period of small vertical oscillation (g = 10, π² ≈ 10):
questions.why: The restoring force per unit displacement is ρAg, so T = 2π√(m/(ρAg)) = 2π√(0.8/(1000 × 10⁻³ × 10)) = 2π√0.08 ≈ 2π × 0.283 ≈ 1.78 s.

questions.q: In SHM, phase difference between displacement and acceleration
questions.why: Since a = −ω²x, the acceleration is opposite to the displacement, so they are π (180°) out of phase.

questions.q: Which graph is a straight line for SHM?
questions.why: In SHM, a = −ω²x, so a vs x is a straight line. The others, v vs x, KE vs x and x vs t, are curves.
