lessons.title: Types of waves and the displacement relation

scenes.text: At a cricket stadium the crowd does a 'Mexican wave' — the wave travels round, but each spectator just stands and sits.
A wave carries energy and pattern, not the medium itself.

steps.title: Types of waves
steps.body:
- **Mechanical** waves need a medium (sound, waves on strings); electromagnetic waves do not.
- **Transverse:** particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of propagation (string waves). Need a medium with shear rigidity, so they do not travel through the bulk of fluids.
- **Longitudinal:** particles oscillate along the direction of propagation — compressions and rarefactions (sound in air).

steps.title: Displacement relation
steps.body:
A wave travelling in +x: **y(x, t) = a sin(kx − ωt + φ)**
- a = amplitude; k = 2π/λ (angular wave number, rad/m)
- ω = 2πν = 2π/T
- **Wave speed v = ω/k = λν**
- A wave in −x direction: y = a sin(kx + ωt + φ).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** y = 0.005 sin(80x − 3t) (SI).
- a = **5 mm**; k = 80 rad/m → λ = 2π/80 ≈ **7.85 cm**
- ω = 3 rad/s → T = 2π/3 ≈ **2.09 s**; v = ω/k = **0.0375 m/s**

**Example 2:** A sound wave of 500 Hz travels at 340 m/s. λ = 340/500 = **0.68 m**.

**Example 3:** Phase difference between two points 0.17 m apart on that wave: Δφ = 2πΔx/λ = 2π × 0.25 = **π/2**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing particle velocity (∂y/∂t) with wave velocity (ω/k).
- Reading k as wavelength.
- Saying sound can be transverse in air.

activity.prompt: Transverse or longitudinal?

quiz.q: Sound waves in air are
quiz.why: Sound in air travels as compressions and rarefactions along the direction of travel, so it is a longitudinal wave.

quiz.q: Wave speed equals
quiz.why: For a travelling wave v = ω/k (the same as λν).

quiz.q: For y = 0.02 sin(2πx − 100πt), the frequency is
quiz.why: Comparing with sin(kx − ωt), ω = 100π rad/s, so ν = ω/2π = 50 Hz.

quiz.q: A wave carries
quiz.why: A wave transports energy; the particles of the medium only oscillate about their positions and are not carried along.

quiz.q: λ for a 680 Hz sound at 340 m/s

lessons.title: Speed of waves: strings and sound

scenes.text: A veena player tightens a peg and the note rises.
More tension means a faster wave on the string and a higher frequency for the same length.

steps.title: Transverse wave on a string
steps.body: **v = √(T/µ)**, T = tension, µ = mass per unit length. Depends only on the string's properties, not on frequency.

steps.title: Longitudinal (sound) waves
steps.body:
- In a fluid: **v = √(B/ρ)**; in a solid rod: v = √(Y/ρ).
- **Newton's formula** (assumed isothermal, B = P): v = √(P/ρ) ≈ 280 m/s for air at STP — too low.
- **Laplace's correction** (adiabatic, B = γP): **v = √(γP/ρ)** ≈ 331 m/s for air at 0 °C ✓.
- v ∝ √T (in kelvin); independent of pressure at constant T; increases with humidity (moist air is less dense).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A string with µ = 0.01 kg/m under 100 N tension: v = √(100/0.01) = **100 m/s**.

**Example 2:** Air at STP (P = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa, ρ = 1.29 kg/m³, γ = 1.4).
- Newton: √(1.01 × 10⁵/1.29) ≈ **280 m/s**
- Laplace: √(1.4 × 1.01 × 10⁵/1.29) ≈ **331 m/s**

**Example 3:** Speed of sound at 0 °C is 331 m/s. At 27 °C: 331 × √(300/273) ≈ **347 m/s**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the string's total mass instead of mass per length.
- Thinking sound speed depends on pressure at constant temperature.
- Using °C in v ∝ √T.

activity.prompt: A wire of mass per length 0.004 kg/m is under 64 N tension. Wave speed in m/s?

quiz.q: Wave speed on a string is
quiz.why: The speed of a transverse wave on a string is v = √(T/μ), where T is tension and μ is mass per unit length.

quiz.q: Laplace corrected Newton by assuming sound propagation is
quiz.why: Newton assumed isothermal compression and got a wrong speed. Laplace showed the compressions are too rapid for heat to flow, so the process is adiabatic.

quiz.q: Tension made 4 times; wave speed becomes
quiz.why: v = √(T/μ) ∝ √T. Four times the tension doubles the wave speed.

quiz.q: Sound travels fastest in
quiz.why: Sound travels fastest in solids such as steel, because of their high elasticity relative to their density.

quiz.q: At constant temperature, doubling air pressure makes sound speed
quiz.why: v = √(γP/ρ), and at constant temperature P/ρ stays the same when P doubles (ρ also doubles). So the speed does not change.

sources: NCERT Physics Class 11 (topic: speed of waves)

scenes.text: A bansuri player covers holes to change the length of the vibrating air column.
A guitarist presses frets to shorten the string. Both select standing-wave patterns of different frequencies.

steps.title: Superposition and reflection
steps.body:
- **Principle of superposition:** net displacement = algebraic sum of individual displacements.
- Reflection at a **rigid boundary:** phase change of π (inverted pulse). At an **open/free boundary:** no phase change.
- Two identical waves in opposite directions form a **standing wave**: y = 2a sin kx cos ωt. **Nodes** (zero amplitude) and **antinodes** (maximum) are λ/2 apart; node to adjacent antinode = λ/4.

steps.title: Normal modes
steps.body:
- **String fixed at both ends** (length L): λₙ = 2L/n, **νₙ = nv/2L**, n = 1, 2, 3… All harmonics.
- **Pipe closed at one end:** node at the closed end, antinode at the open end: **ν = (2n − 1)v/4L** — only odd harmonics.
- **Pipe open at both ends:** antinodes at both ends: **ν = nv/2L** — all harmonics.
- Fundamental = first harmonic; higher modes are overtones.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A 0.5 m open pipe, v = 340 m/s. Fundamental = 340/(2 × 0.5) = **340 Hz**; next harmonics 680, 1020 Hz.

**Example 2:** Same length closed at one end: fundamental = 340/(4 × 0.5) = **170 Hz**; next allowed 510, 850 Hz (odd multiples).

**Example 3:** A 1 m string with wave speed 200 m/s: ν₁ = 200/2 = **100 Hz**; third harmonic **300 Hz**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Allowing even harmonics in a closed pipe.
- Using λ = L for the fundamental of a string (it is 2L).
- Forgetting the inversion on reflection from a rigid end.

activity.prompt: Match the system to its fundamental frequency
pairs: String fixed at both ends, length L
Pipe open at both ends, length L
Pipe closed at one end, length L

quiz.q: Distance between adjacent nodes
quiz.why: In a standing wave, adjacent nodes are separated by half a wavelength, λ/2.

quiz.q: A closed pipe produces
quiz.why: A pipe closed at one end has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so only odd harmonics are possible.

quiz.q: Reflection from a rigid end causes a phase change of
quiz.why: On reflection from a fixed or rigid end the wave is inverted, which is a phase change of π.

quiz.q: Fundamental of a 0.85 m closed pipe (v = 340 m/s)
quiz.why: The fundamental of a closed pipe is v/4L = 340/(4 × 0.85) = 340/3.4 = 100 Hz.

quiz.q: An open pipe and a closed pipe of the same length: ratio of fundamentals (open : closed)
quiz.why: An open pipe has fundamental v/2L and a closed pipe has v/4L. The ratio open : closed is 2 : 1.

scenes.text: A harmonium tuner plays a reed together with a tuning fork and hears 'wah-wah-wah'.
He adjusts until the wavering stops — beats vanish when frequencies match.

steps.title: Beats
steps.body:
Two waves of slightly different frequencies ν₁ and ν₂ superpose to give a loudness that rises and falls periodically.
- **Beat frequency = |ν₁ − ν₂|**
- Resultant: s = [2a cos(πΔν t)] cos(2π ν_avg t) — a tone at the average frequency with slowly varying amplitude.
- Ear distinguishes beats up to about 10 per second.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Forks of 256 Hz and 260 Hz → **4 beats/s**.

**Example 2:** A fork of unknown frequency gives 5 beats/s with a 400 Hz fork. On loading the unknown fork with wax (lowers its frequency), beats become 3/s. Unknown frequency?
- Possible: 405 or 395 Hz. Loading lowers it; if 405 → 403 → beats 3 ✓; if 395 → lower → beats increase ✗.
- Answer **405 Hz**.

**Example 3:** Filing a fork's prongs RAISES its frequency — use the same logic in reverse.

steps.title: JEE bridge: Doppler effect
steps.body: When source or listener moves, the observed frequency changes: ν' = ν (v + v_L)/(v − v_S) for approach (v = speed of sound, v_L listener speed toward source, v_S source speed toward listener). A passing ambulance siren drops in pitch as it goes by.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that beats give only the DIFFERENCE, so two answers are possible until extra information is used.
- Mixing up loading (frequency down) and filing (frequency up).
- Applying beats to frequencies that differ a lot (then you hear two separate notes).

a.text: Fork A is 512 Hz. Fork B gives 6 beats/s with A. You put a little wax on B and now hear 4 beats/s. What is B's original frequency?

choices.label: 506 Hz
choices.feedback: Wax would lower 506 further, increasing the beats above 6.

wrong.text: Think again: loading lowers frequency. Only 518 Hz is consistent with fewer beats.

quiz.q: Beat frequency of 300 Hz and 304 Hz
quiz.why: The beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies: 304 − 300 = 4 Hz.

quiz.q: Loading a tuning fork with wax
quiz.why: Wax adds mass to the prong, which lowers the frequency of the tuning fork.

quiz.q: Beats are a result of
quiz.why: Beats arise from the superposition of two waves of nearly equal frequency, which alternately reinforce and cancel.

quiz.q: Perceived pitch while beats occur corresponds to
quiz.why: While beating, the sound heard has the average of the two frequencies, with its loudness rising and falling at the beat frequency.

quiz.q: As an ambulance moves away from you, its siren pitch
quiz.why: By the Doppler effect, a source moving away makes the observer hear a lower frequency, so the pitch falls.

questions.q: Which needs a medium?
questions.why: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a medium. Light, X-rays and radio waves can travel through vacuum.

questions.q: k = 2π/λ is called
questions.why: The quantity k = 2π/λ is called the angular wave number (or propagation constant).

questions.q: Speed of sound at STP is about
questions.why: The speed of sound in air at STP (0 °C) is about 331 m/s, using Laplace's adiabatic correction.

questions.q: y = 0.1 sin(10πx − 400πt). Wave speed:
questions.why: Wave speed v = ω/k = 400π/10π = 40 m/s.

questions.q: Assertion: Transverse waves cannot travel through the interior of a gas. Reason: Gases have no shear rigidity.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Transverse waves need a restoring force against shear, and gases have no rigidity (no shear modulus), so they cannot support transverse waves.

questions.q: Distance between a node and the adjacent antinode
questions.why: In a standing wave, a node and the next antinode are λ/4 apart.

questions.q: A string's tension is increased by 44%. Its fundamental frequency rises by
questions.why: ν ∝ √T. If T becomes 1.44 times, the frequency becomes √1.44 = 1.2 times, a rise of 20%.

questions.q: Case: A 34 cm pipe closed at one end (v = 340 m/s). Its first two resonant frequencies are
questions.why: For a pipe closed at one end, ν₁ = v/4L = 340/(4 × 0.34) = 250 Hz. The next resonance is the third harmonic, 3 × 250 = 750 Hz.

questions.q: Ratio of speed of sound in hydrogen to oxygen at the same T (both diatomic):
questions.why: v = √(γRT/M), so at the same T and γ, v ∝ 1/√M. H₂ is 16 times lighter than O₂, so its speed of sound is √16 = 4 times larger: 4 : 1.

questions.q: An open pipe's 2nd harmonic equals a closed pipe's fundamental. Ratio of lengths (open : closed):
questions.why: The open pipe's 2nd harmonic is 2 × v/2L₀ = v/L₀, and the closed pipe's fundamental is v/4L_c. Equating gives L₀ = 4L_c, so the ratio is 4 : 1.

questions.q: Fork P (unknown) gives 4 beats/s with a 256 Hz fork. Filing P makes beats 6/s. P's frequency was
questions.why: 4 beats with 256 Hz means P was 252 or 260 Hz. Filing raises P's frequency. If P were 260, the beats would go up to 6 (as observed), whereas from 252 they would fall to 2 or fewer, so P was 260 Hz.

questions.q: A sonometer wire of length 1 m vibrates at 256 Hz. Length for 384 Hz (same tension):
questions.why: For a string at fixed tension ν ∝ 1/L, so L = 1 × 256/384 = 0.667 m.

questions.q: A steel wire 0.72 m long, mass 5 × 10⁻³ kg, under 72 N tension vibrates in its fundamental. Frequency:
Two waves y₁ = a sin(kx − ωt), y₂ = a sin(kx + ωt) superpose. Amplitude at x = λ/8:
questions.why: The sum is a standing wave 2a sin kx cos ωt. At x = λ/8, kx = 2π/λ × λ/8 = π/4, so the amplitude is 2a sin(π/4) = 2a/√2 = √2 a.

questions.q: Speed of sound at 0 °C is 332 m/s. Temperature at which it doubles:
questions.why: v ∝ √T (kelvin). For v to double, T must become four times: 4 × 273 = 1092 K = 819 °C.

questions.q: Which is a longitudinal wave?
questions.why: Sound in air is a longitudinal wave (compressions and rarefactions). Light, waves on a rope and surface ripples are mainly transverse.

scenes.text: Pooja has one evening before her unit test and twelve chapters of notes.
She compresses each chapter to its five most-used formulas and checks units for each.

steps.title: Units, kinematics, vectors
steps.body:
- % error of Z = AᵖBᑫ/Cʳ: p%A + q%B + r%C
- v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; sₙ = u + a(2n − 1)/2
- R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ)
- Projectile: T = 2u sin θ/g, H = u² sin² θ/2g, R = u² sin 2θ/g
- Circular: a = v²/r = ω²r

steps.title: Laws of motion, work–energy
steps.body:
- F = dp/dt; impulse = Δp
- f_s ≤ µₛN; f_k = µ_kN; tan θ_repose = µₛ
- Level curve v_max = √(µRg); banked v₀ = √(Rg tan θ)
- W = F·d; K = p²/2m; spring U = ½kx²; P = F·v
- Elastic 1D (m₂ at rest): v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u/(m₁ + m₂), v₂ = 2m₁u/(m₁ + m₂)

steps.title: Rotation and gravitation
steps.body:
- X_cm = Σmx/Σm; τ = r × F; L = Iω; τ = Iα; KE_rot = ½Iω²
- I: ring MR², disc ½MR², sphere (2/5)MR², rod ML²/12 (centre), ML²/3 (end)
- F = Gm₁m₂/r²; g = GM/R²; g_h ≈ g(1 − 2h/R); g_d = g(1 − d/R)
- vₑ = √(2gR); v₀ = √(GM/r); T² ∝ r³; E = −GMm/2r

steps.title: Strategy
steps.body:
- Draw a diagram for every mechanics question — FBD, vector triangle or v–t graph.
- Check dimensions of your final expression.
- Do limiting-case checks (m₁ = m₂, θ = 0, h → 0).

quiz.q: Dimensions of angular momentum
quiz.why: Angular momentum = r × p, so its dimensions are [L][M L T⁻¹] = [M L² T⁻¹].

quiz.q: A ball thrown up at 15 m/s (g = 10) returns after
quiz.why: A ball thrown up at u returns to the starting height after 2u/g = 2 × 15/10 = 3 s.

quiz.q: Momentum conservation follows from Newton's
quiz.why: Momentum conservation follows from Newton's second law (F = dp/dt) and third law (internal forces are equal and opposite and cancel).

quiz.q: KE of a body is increased by 300%. Its momentum increases by
quiz.why: KE rises by 300%, so the new KE is 4 times the old one. Since p = √(2mK), the momentum becomes √4 = 2 times, an increase of 100%.

quiz.q: g at depth R/2 vs height R/2 (ratio depth : height)
quiz.why: At depth R/2, g′ = g/2. At height R/2, g′ = g/(1.5)² = 4g/9. Ratio = (1/2)/(4/9) = 9/8.

quiz.q: I of a disc about its diameter (perpendicular-axis theorem)
quiz.why: By the perpendicular-axis theorem, I_z = I_x + I_y = 2I_d, and I_z = MR²/2 for a disc. So I_d = MR²/4.

scenes.text: Four friends split the thermal chapters and each teaches one to the others.
Teaching forces them to state each formula with its conditions — when it applies and when it doesn't.

steps.title: Solids and fluids
steps.body:
- Y = FL/(AΔL); B = −p/(ΔV/V); energy density ½ stress × strain
- P = Pₐ + ρgh; Pascal: F₂ = F₁A₂/A₁
- A₁v₁ = A₂v₂; P + ½ρv² + ρgh = const; Torricelli v = √(2gh)
- F = 6πηrv; v_t = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/9η; Re = ρvd/η
- Drop 2S/r; soap bubble 4S/r; h = 2S cos θ/ρgr

steps.title: Heat and thermodynamics
steps.body:
- ΔL = αLΔT; β = 2α; γ = 3α
- Q = mcΔT; Q = mL
- H = KAΔT/L; P = eσAT⁴; λₘT = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K
- ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW; Cₚ − C_v = R
- Isothermal W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁); adiabatic PV^γ = const, W = nR(T₁ − T₂)/(γ − 1)
- η = 1 − T₂/T₁ (Carnot); COP = T₂/(T₁ − T₂)

steps.title: Kinetic theory
steps.body:
- PV = nRT = Nk_BT
- P = (1/3)ρ⟨v²⟩; KE_avg = (3/2)k_BT
- v_rms = √(3RT/M)
- C_v = (f/2)R; γ = 1 + 2/f
- λ = 1/(√2πd²n)

steps.title: Top exam traps
steps.body:
- Kelvin vs Celsius in gas laws, Stefan's law and Carnot.
- Soap bubble has two surfaces.
- ΔU = nC_vΔT for every process of an ideal gas.

activity.prompt: Match the formula to its law

quiz.q: Water rises 4 cm in a capillary. In a tube of half the radius it rises
quiz.why: Capillary rise h ∝ 1/r. Halving the radius doubles the rise to 8 cm.

quiz.q: Efficiency of a Carnot engine between 400 K and 300 K
Two drops of water combine. Surface energy
quiz.why: When two drops merge, the total surface area decreases, so the surface energy decreases and the extra energy is released as heat.

quiz.q: v_rms at 27 °C is 500 m/s. At 927 °C it is
quiz.why: v_rms ∝ √T. Going from 27 °C (300 K) to 927 °C (1200 K) multiplies it by √4 = 2, so 1000 m/s.

quiz.q: For an adiabatic process
quiz.why: An adiabatic process is one with no heat exchange with the surroundings, so ΔQ = 0.

quiz.q: Thermal stress in a clamped rod
quiz.why: A clamped rod cannot expand, so the prevented strain is αΔT. Thermal stress = Y × strain = YαΔT.

scenes.text: In the mock, Imran wasted 40 minutes on one hard question and could not finish.
Next time he does a first pass of easy questions, marks hard ones, and returns — scoring 20 marks more.

steps.title: Oscillations
steps.body:
- x = A cos(ωt + φ); v = ω√(A² − x²); a = −ω²x
- E = ½kA²; KE = PE at x = A/√2
- Spring T = 2π√(m/k); pendulum T = 2π√(L/g)
- Series 1/k = Σ1/kᵢ; parallel k = Σkᵢ

steps.title: Waves
steps.body:
- y = a sin(kx − ωt); v = ω/k = λν
- String v = √(T/µ); gas v = √(γP/ρ) ∝ √T
- String/open pipe νₙ = nv/2L; closed pipe ν = (2n − 1)v/4L
- Beats = |ν₁ − ν₂|

steps.title: Exam strategy
steps.body:
- **First pass (≈ 40% of time):** all 1- and 2-mark questions and easy numericals.
- **Second pass:** long answers/derivations — write the statement, diagram, steps, final boxed result with units.
- **Third pass:** hardest numericals; partial working earns marks in boards.
- In MCQ entrance tests, eliminate options using dimensions and limiting cases; skip if unsure when negative marking applies.

steps.title: Last-minute checks
steps.body:
- Units in every final answer.
- Significant figures consistent with data.
- Vector directions stated (east, upward, toward centre).

activity.prompt: Exam-day checklist
items: Revise the three formula sheets once
Sleep at least 7 hours
Carry admit card, pens, pencil, scale, eraser
Read the whole paper in the first 10 minutes
Attempt easy questions first
Leave 10 minutes to recheck units and answers

quiz.q: Pendulum of length 1 m on Earth (g ≈ π²) has period
quiz.why: With g ≈ π², T = 2π√(L/g) = 2π√(1/π²) = 2 s (which is why a 1 m pendulum is nearly a seconds pendulum).

quiz.q: Fundamental of a string doubles when its length is
quiz.why: For a string, the fundamental frequency is ν ∝ 1/L, so it doubles when the length is halved.

quiz.q: The best first step in a mechanics problem is usually
quiz.why: Drawing a diagram or free-body diagram organises the information and forces, and is usually the best first step in a mechanics problem.

quiz.q: Total energy in SHM if amplitude triples
quiz.why: SHM energy E = ½kA² ∝ A². If the amplitude triples, the energy becomes 9 times.

quiz.q: Beats heard with 440 Hz and 437 Hz
quiz.why: The beat frequency equals the difference of the frequencies: 440 − 437 = 3 beats per second.

lessons.title: Mock paper 1 (mixed, timed)

scenes.text: Set a timer, keep the formula sheet away, and attempt these questions in one sitting.
Then read each explanation — the mistakes you make today are the marks you gain tomorrow.

steps.title: How to use this mock
steps.body:
- Time limit: about 1.5 minutes per question.
- No calculator for simple arithmetic — practise approximations (√2 ≈ 1.41, π² ≈ 10, g ≈ 10).
- Mark doubtful questions and come back.

steps.title: Approximation toolkit
steps.body:
- (1 + x)ⁿ ≈ 1 + nx for small x
- sin θ ≈ tan θ ≈ θ (radians) for small angles
- ln 2 ≈ 0.693, log₁₀ 2 ≈ 0.301

steps.title: After the mock
steps.body: Make an error log with three columns: concept gap, careless slip, time pressure. Fix concept gaps by re-doing that chapter's lesson; fix slips by writing units and signs every time.

activity.prompt: After the mock paper: which two chapters cost you the most marks, and what is your plan for each?
activity.hint: Be specific: e.g. 'Rotation — revise moment of inertia table, do 10 problems on τ = Iα by Sunday.'

quiz.q: A car moving at 72 km/h stops in 4 s. Deceleration:
quiz.why: 72 km/h = 20 m/s. Deceleration = Δv/t = 20/4 = 5 m/s².

quiz.q: Two masses 2 kg and 8 kg have equal KE. Ratio of momenta (2 kg : 8 kg):
quiz.why: For equal KE, p = √(2mK) ∝ √m. The ratio of momenta is √2 : √8 = 1 : 2.

quiz.q: A satellite orbits at height R. Its period relative to a near-surface satellite (84 min):
quiz.why: By Kepler's third law, T ∝ r^(3/2). At height R the radius is 2R, so T = 2^(1.5) × 84 ≈ 2.83 × 84 ≈ 238 min.

quiz.q: Heat needed to raise 1 mol of a monatomic gas by 10 K at constant volume (R = 8.3):
quiz.why: At constant volume, Q = nCvΔT = 1 × (3/2)(8.3) × 10 = 124.5 J.

quiz.q: A closed pipe resonates at 300 Hz and 500 Hz consecutively. Its fundamental is
quiz.why: A closed pipe has only odd harmonics, so consecutive resonant frequencies differ by 2ν₁. Here 500 − 300 = 200, so ν₁ = 100 Hz.

quiz.q: A wire extends 1 mm under a load. The same load on a wire of the same material, double length and double radius, gives
quiz.why: The extension ΔL = FL/(πr²Y) ∝ L/r². Double length and double radius give 2/4 = 1/2, so the extension is 0.5 mm.

quiz.q: Torque on a body is zero. Which must be constant?
quiz.why: Since τ = dL/dt, zero torque means the angular momentum is constant. KE or linear momentum need not remain constant.

quiz.q: A body moves under F = −16x with m = 1 kg. Its period:
quiz.why: F = −16x with m = 1 kg gives ω² = 16, so ω = 4 rad/s. T = 2π/ω = 2π/4 = π/2 s.

sources: Original mock questions based on the NCERT Class 11 Physics syllabus

questions.q: Mock 2 · Number of significant figures in 3.0800
questions.why: In 3.0800, all digits are significant including the trailing zeros after the decimal point, giving 5 significant figures.

questions.q: Mock 2 · SI unit of coefficient of viscosity
questions.why: The coefficient of viscosity has unit Pa s (N s m⁻²), from Newton's law of viscosity F = ηA dv/dx.

questions.q: Mock 2 · A body is thrown horizontally. Its horizontal velocity
questions.why: There is no horizontal force on a projectile, so its horizontal velocity stays constant while the vertical velocity changes under gravity.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Unit of Stefan's constant
questions.why: From P = σAT⁴, σ = P/(AT⁴), so its unit is W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Momentum of a 10 g bullet at 300 m/s
questions.why: Momentum = mass × velocity = 0.01 kg × 300 m/s = 3 kg m/s (10 g converted to 0.01 kg).

questions.q: Mock 2 · Assertion: The surface of a liquid behaves like a stretched membrane. Reason: Surface molecules have extra energy and the surface tends to contract.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Surface molecules have extra energy and the surface tends to shrink to the smallest area, so it behaves like a stretched membrane, which is surface tension.

questions.q: Mock 2 · A projectile is fired at 60°. At the top its KE is what fraction of the initial KE?
questions.why: At the top only the horizontal velocity u cos 60° remains. KE ∝ v², so the fraction is cos²60° = (1/2)² = 1/4.

questions.q: Mock 2 · A man pushes a wall but it does not move. Work done by him on the wall:
questions.why: Work needs displacement. The wall does not move, so the man does zero work on it, however tired he gets.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Moment of inertia of a uniform rod (2 kg, 3 m) about its centre (⟂)
questions.why: For a rod about its centre, I = ML²/12 = 2 × 9/12 = 1.5 kg m².

questions.q: Mock 2 · An ideal gas is compressed isothermally. Heat is
questions.why: In isothermal compression ΔU = 0, so the work done on the gas is released as heat. The gas gives out heat.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Case: A lift of mass 500 kg accelerates upward at 2 m/s² (g = 10). Cable tension:
questions.why: For a lift accelerating upward, T − mg = ma, so T = m(g + a) = 500 × 12 = 6000 N.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Two wires of the same material, radii in ratio 1:2, lengths in ratio 2:1, carry the same load. Ratio of strains:
questions.why: Strain = F/(AY) ∝ 1/r² for the same load and material (length does not matter). Radii in ratio 1 : 2 give strains in ratio 4 : 1.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Ratio of escape speed to orbital speed for a satellite orbiting just above the surface
questions.why: Escape speed √(2gR) divided by orbital speed √(gR) just above the surface is √2.

questions.q: Mock 2 · A ball is dropped from 80 m. Distance covered in the last second (g = 10):
questions.why: From 80 m, fall time t = √(2h/g) = 4 s. Distance in the 4th second = g(2n − 1)/2 = 10 × 7/2 = 35 m.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Water flows through a horizontal pipe: at A (area 4 cm²) speed 1 m/s; at B (area 1 cm²). Pressure difference P_A − P_B (ρ = 1000):
questions.why: By continuity v_B = 4 × 1 = 4 m/s. By Bernoulli, P_A − P_B = ½ρ(v_B² − v_A²) = ½ × 1000 × (16 − 1) = 7500 Pa.

questions.q: Mock 2 · A Carnot engine of efficiency 40% has its sink at 300 K. To raise efficiency to 50%, the source temperature must rise by
questions.why: At 40% efficiency, 1 − 300/T₁ = 0.4, so T₁ = 500 K. At 50%, 1 − 300/T₁ = 0.5, so T₁ = 600 K. The source temperature must rise by 100 K.

questions.q: Mock 2 · A 2 kg block on a smooth floor is attached to a spring (k = 50 N/m) and pulled 0.2 m. Maximum speed:
questions.why: ω = √(k/m) = √(50/2) = 5 rad/s. The maximum speed is Aω = 0.2 × 5 = 1 m/s.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Two simple pendulums of lengths 1 m and 1.21 m start swinging together in phase. After how many oscillations of the shorter one will they be in phase again?
questions.why: T ∝ √L, so the periods are in the ratio 1 : 1.1. When the shorter one has made 11 oscillations the longer has made 10, so they are in phase again after 11 oscillations of the shorter pendulum.

questions.q: Mock 2 · A uniform chain of length L lies on a smooth table with length l hanging over the edge. Work needed to pull the hanging part back (mass M):
questions.why: The hanging part has mass Ml/L and its centre of mass is l/2 below the table. Raising it by l/2 needs W = (Ml/L) g (l/2) = Mgl²/2L.

questions.q: Mock 2 · A gas with γ = 1.5 expands adiabatically to 4 times its volume. Its absolute temperature becomes
questions.why: For an adiabatic process TV^(γ−1) is constant. With γ = 1.5 and V → 4V, T₂ = T₁(1/4)^0.5 = T₁/2.
